figures.cap: increasing concave-down curve through O with point at x=1

solutions.latex:
At $x=1$ the curve is above the axis, increasing and concave down, so $f(1)>0$, $f'(1)>0$ and $f''(1)<0$.

The curve starts at the origin and its gradient is decreasing, so the gradient at $x=1$ is less than the gradient of the chord from $O$, which is $\dfrac{f(1)}{1}$. So $f'(1)<f(1)$:
$$f''(1)<0<f'(1)<f(1)$$

parts.latex: Sketch the graph of the curve $y=-x^3+3x^2-1$, labelling the stationary points and point of inflection. Do NOT determine the $x$ intercepts of the curve.

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned} y &= -x^3 + 3x^2 - 1 \\ \dfrac{dy}{dx} &= -3x^2 + 6x \\ &= 3x(2 - x) \end{aligned}$$
When $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 0$, we have $3x(2-x) = 0$.
$$x = 0, \qquad x = 2$$
$$y = -1 \qquad y = -2^3 + 3(2)^2 - 1 = 3$$
Stationary points are $(0, -1)$ and $(2, 3)$.
$$\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} = -6x + 6$$
When $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} = 0$, we have $6(1-x) = 0$.
$$x = 1$$
$$\begin{aligned} y &= -1^3 + 3\times 1^2 - 1 \\ &= 1 \end{aligned}$$
The point of inflection is $(1, 1)$.

parts.latex: Show that $f''(x)=4(x-1)e^{-2x}$.

criteria: Attempts to use the product rule

solutions.latex:
Stationary points where $f'(x) = 0$
$$(1 - 2x)e^{-2x} = 0$$
$$x = \dfrac{1}{2}, \qquad \text{since } e^{-2x} \neq 0$$
$$\begin{aligned} f\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) &= \dfrac{1}{2}e^{-1} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2e} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} f''\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) &= 4 \times -\dfrac{1}{2} \times e^{-1} \\ &= -2e^{-1} \\ &< 0 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \left(\dfrac{1}{2}, \dfrac{1}{2e}\right) \text{ is a local maximum.}$$
criteria: Finds the $x$ value of the stationary point

Possible point of inflection where $f''(x) = 0$

$$\therefore\ x = 1, \qquad \text{since } e^{-2x} \neq 0$$
\extable{Ts212_1}

Changes concavity at $x = 1$.

$\therefore$ Inflection point at $x = 1$
$$\begin{aligned} f(1) &= 1e^{-2 \times 1} \\ &= e^{-2} \end{aligned}$$

figures.cap: graph of y=f'(x) with x-values a, b, c marked

solutions.latex:
Read the features of $f(x)$ from the graph of $y=f'(x)$:

At $x=a$, $f'(x)=0$ and changes from positive to negative, so $f(x)$ has a maximum turning point there (A is false).

At $x=b$, $f'(x)$ has a minimum turning point, so $f''(x)=0$ and $f''(x)$ changes from negative to positive: the concavity of $f(x)$ changes, so $f(x)$ has a point of inflection at $x=b$.

At $x=c$, $f'(x)=0$ and changes from negative to positive, so $f(x)$ has a minimum turning point there, not a maximum or a point of inflection (C and D are false).

$\therefore$ $f(x)$ has a point of inflection at $x=b$.

parts.latex: For what values of $b$ is the function $y=x^4+bx^3-3x^2$ concave up and decreasing at the point where $x=1$?

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned} y' &= 4x^3 + 3bx^2 - 6x \\ y'' &= 12x^2 + 6bx - 6 \end{aligned}$$
Decreasing at $x = 1$:
$$\begin{aligned} 4 + 3b - 6 &< 0 \\ b &< \dfrac{2}{3} \end{aligned}$$
Concave up at $x = 1$:
$$\begin{aligned} 12 + 6b - 6 &> 0 \\ b &> -1 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ -1 < b < \dfrac{2}{3}, \text{ that is } b \in \left(-1, \dfrac{2}{3}\right)$$

parts.latex:
Consider the function $f(x)=\dfrac{4x}{\sqrt{x-2}}$.

Find any stationary points and determine their nature.

solutions.latex:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=4x & v&=\sqrt{x-2}\\ u'&=4 & v'&=\dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{x-2}}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}f'(x)&=\dfrac{4\sqrt{x-2}-\frac{4x}{2\sqrt{x-2}}}{x-2}\\ &=\dfrac{4\sqrt{x-2}-\frac{2x}{\sqrt{x-2}}}{x-2}\end{aligned}$$
Solve $f'(x)=0$ to find any stationary points:
$$\begin{aligned}4\sqrt{x-2}-\dfrac{2x}{\sqrt{x-2}}&=0\\ 4(x-2)-2x&=0\\ 4x-8-2x&=0\\ 2x&=8\end{aligned}$$
Hence $x=4$.
$$f(x)=\dfrac{4\times 4}{\sqrt{4-2}}=8\sqrt{2}$$
A stationary point exists at $(4,8\sqrt{2})$.

solutions.latex:
We need a point that is below the $x$-axis ($f < 0$), on an increasing part of the curve ($f' > 0$) and where the curve is concave down ($f'' < 0$).

$A$: below the axis, the curve is rising towards the maximum, and it is concave down there. All three conditions hold.

$B$: $f(x) > 0$. Fails.

$C$: $f'(x) < 0$ (the curve is still falling to its minimum). Fails.

$D$: below the axis and rising, but concave up (after the minimum). Fails.

Product rule.reason: f' is a product of e^{−x} and (1−x)

parts.latex:
Hence sketch the curve.

\exfigure{568_q14_1}

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=2x & v&=e^{-x}\\ u'&=2 & v'&=-e^{-x}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x) &= 2e^{-x} + 2x(-e^{-x}) \\ &= 2e^{-x} - 2xe^{-x} \\ &= 2e^{-x}(1-x) \end{aligned}$$

Stationary points occur where $f'(x) = 0$.

Since $2e^{-x} > 0$ for all $x$, we need $1 - x = 0$, so $x = 1$.

$f(1) = 2e^{-1} = \dfrac{2}{e}$.

Nature:
$$\begin{aligned} f''(x) &= -2e^{-x}(1-x) - 2e^{-x} \\ &= 2e^{-x}(x-2) \end{aligned}$$
$f''(1) = 2e^{-1}(-1) = -\dfrac{2}{e} < 0$, so the curve is concave down there.

$\therefore$ $\left(1, \dfrac{2}{e}\right)$ is a maximum turning point.
criteria: Finds $x=1$ and the stationary point $\left(1,\dfrac{2}{e}\right)$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
$f(x) = \dfrac{2x}{e^x}$. As $x \to \infty$, $e^x$ grows much faster than $2x$, so
$$\lim_{x \to \infty} 2xe^{-x} = 0$$

$f''(x) = 2e^{-x}(x-2)$.

Since $2e^{-x} > 0$, $f''(x) = 0$ only when $x = 2$.

Check the change in concavity:
$$\begin{aligned} f''(1) &= -2e^{-1} < 0 &&\text{concave down}\\ f''(3) &= 2e^{-3} > 0 &&\text{concave up} \end{aligned}$$
The sign changes, so it is a point of inflection.
$$f(2) = 4e^{-2}$$
$\therefore$ The point of inflection is $\left(2, \dfrac{4}{e^2}\right)$.

meta.top_criterion_original: Concavity changes, so the point of inflection is $\left(2, \dfrac{4}{e^2}\right)$

parts.latex: If $y=\ln(1+\sin x)$ for $0\le x\le \pi$, show that $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}+e^{-y}=0$ .
Use the result in part (a) to determine the concavity of the curve for $0\le x\le \pi$.

solutions.latex:
$y=\ln(1+\sin x)$
$$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{\cos x}{1+\sin x}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}&=\dfrac{-\sin x(1+\sin x)-\cos x\cdot\cos x}{(1+\sin x)^2}\\ &=\dfrac{-(\sin^2x+\cos^2x)-\sin x}{(1+\sin x)^2}\\ &=\dfrac{-(1+\sin x)}{(1+\sin x)^2}\\ &=\dfrac{-1}{(1+\sin x)}\\ &=\dfrac{-1}{e^y}\\ &=-e^{-y}\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}+e^{-y}=0$$

parts.latex: Find the coordinates and nature of any stationary points on the curve $y=\dfrac{a}{x}+\ln x$ for $x>0$, where $a>0$ is a constant.

solutions.latex:
$y=\dfrac{a}{x}+\ln x$
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dy}{dx}&=\dfrac{-a}{x^2}+\dfrac{1}{x}\\ &=\dfrac{x-a}{x^2}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dy}{dx}&=0 &&\text{when } x=a &&\text{stationary}\\ \dfrac{dy}{dx}&<0 &&\text{for } 0<x<a &&\text{decreasing}\\ \dfrac{dy}{dx}&>0 &&\text{for } x>a &&\text{increasing}\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore\ (a,\ 1+\ln a)$ is a minimum turning point.

parts.latex: Let $f(x)=x^3-3x^2+2$. In which domain is the function decreasing and concave down?

solutions.latex:
Decreasing: $f'(x)<0$
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x)&=3x^2-6x\\ &=3x(x-2) \end{aligned}$$
$f'(x)<0$ for $0<x<2$.

Concave down: $f''(x)<0$
$$f''(x)=6x-6$$
$f''(x)<0$ for $x<1$.

Both hold for $0<x<1$.

$\therefore$ The function is decreasing and concave down on $(0,1)$.

parts.latex: Find the stationary points of the function and determine their nature.

solutions.latex:
$$f(x)=\dfrac{x^2}{e^x}$$
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x^2 & v&=e^x\\ u'&=2x & v'&=e^x\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x) &= \dfrac{2xe^x-x^2e^x}{e^{2x}}\\ &= \dfrac{xe^x(2-x)}{e^{2x}} \\ &= \dfrac{x(2-x)}{e^x} \end{aligned}$$
Stationary points where $f'(x)=0$. Since $e^x>0$:
$$x=0 \text{ or } x=2$$
$$\begin{aligned} f(0) &= 0\\ f(2) &= \dfrac{4}{e^2}=0.541\ldots\end{aligned}$$
\extable{Ts602_1}
$$\therefore\ \text{Minimum at } (0,0) \text{ and maximum at } \left(2,\dfrac{4}{e^2}\right)$$

parts.latex:
Let $y=4x^3-3x^2-6x+d$, where $d$ is a real number.

Use differential calculus to find the values of $d$ for which this curve has exactly three $x$-intercepts. (Note: You do NOT need to find the $x$-intercepts.)

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dy}{dx}&=12x^2-6x-6\\ &=6(2x+1)(x-1)\end{aligned}$$
Stationary points where $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=0$: $x=-\dfrac{1}{2}$ or $x=1$.
$$\begin{aligned} y\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right)&=4\left(-\dfrac{1}{8}\right)-3\left(\dfrac{1}{4}\right)+3+d=d+\dfrac{7}{4}\\ y(1)&=4-3-6+d=d-5\end{aligned}$$
Nature, using $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=24x-6$:
$$\begin{aligned} x&=-\dfrac{1}{2}: &\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}&=-18<0 &&\text{local maximum}\\ x&=1: &\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}&=18>0 &&\text{local minimum}\end{aligned}$$
The cubic has exactly three $x$-intercepts when its local maximum is above the $x$-axis and its local minimum is below it:
$$\begin{aligned} d+\dfrac{7}{4}&>0 &&\text{so } d>-\dfrac{7}{4}\\ d-5&<0 &&\text{so } d<5\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ -\dfrac{7}{4}<d<5$$

parts.latex: The function $y=e^x\cos 2x$ has a stationary point at $x=0.23$ and $x=1.80$ (correct to 2 decimal places). Find the point of inflection of the function $y=e^x\cos 2x$ for $0.23<x<1.80$.

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=e^x & v&=\cos 2x\\ u'&=e^x & v'&=-2\sin 2x\end{aligned}$$
$$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=-2e^x\sin 2x+e^x\cos 2x$$
Differentiate each term with the product rule again. For $-2e^x\sin 2x$:
$$\begin{aligned} u&=-2e^x & v&=\sin 2x\\ u'&=-2e^x & v'&=2\cos 2x\end{aligned}$$
For $e^x\cos 2x$:
$$\begin{aligned} u&=e^x & v&=\cos 2x\\ u'&=e^x & v'&=-2\sin 2x\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}&=-4e^x\cos 2x-2e^x\sin 2x-2e^x\sin 2x+e^x\cos 2x\\&=-3e^x\cos 2x-4e^x\sin 2x\end{aligned}$$
Possible points of inflection occur when $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}-3e^x\cos 2x-4e^x\sin 2x&=0\\-e^x(3\cos 2x+4\sin 2x)&=0\\3\cos 2x+4\sin 2x&=0\quad\text{since } e^x>0\\3\cos 2x&=-4\sin 2x\\\dfrac{\sin 2x}{\cos 2x}&=\dfrac{-3}{4}\\\tan 2x&=\dfrac{-3}{4}\end{aligned}$$
For $0.23<x<1.80$, $0.46<2x<3.60$, and $\tan 2x<0$, so $2x$ is in the second quadrant:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{reference angle}&=0.6435011088\\2x&=\pi-0.6435011088\\&=2.498091545\\x&=1.249045772\\&=1.25\ (2\text{ decimal places})\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}y&=e^{1.249045772}\cos(2\times1.249045772)\\&=-2.789611172\\&=-2.79\ (2\text{ decimal places})\end{aligned}$$
Check that the concavity changes either side of $x=1.25$:

\exfigure{1356_q21_s1}

$\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}$ changes sign, so there is a point of inflection at $(1.25,-2.79)$.
criteria: Correctly finds the reference angle, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Find the first derivative of $f(x)$.
Hence, find the second derivative of $f(x)$.
By identifying a pattern, write down an expression for the $n$th derivative of $f(x)$, where $n$ is a positive integer.

Product rule.reason: Differentiating e^x(x+1) needs the product rule to find the pattern.

Second derivative.reason: Pattern for nth derivative requires computing higher derivatives.

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=e^x & v&=x+1 \\ u'&=e^x & v'&=1 \end{aligned}$$
$$f'(x)=e^x(x+1)+e^x$$

Differentiate $f'(x)=e^x(x+1)+e^x$, using part (a) for the first term:
$$\begin{aligned} f''(x)&=e^x(x+1)+e^x+e^x \\ &=e^x(x+1)+2e^x \\ &=e^x(x+3) \end{aligned}$$

Each derivative adds another $e^x$: $f'(x)=e^x(x+2)$, $f''(x)=e^x(x+3)$, so
$$\dfrac{d^n}{dx^n}\,e^x(x+1)=e^x(x+n+1)$$

$$f'(x)=-3x^2+12x$$
Stationary points occur where $f'(x)=0$:

$$f''(4)=-6\times4+12=-12<0 \text{ (concave down)}$$
$\therefore$ $(4,31)$ is a maximum turning point.

parts.latex:
Sketch the curve $y=\dfrac{x^3}{6}+\dfrac{x^2}{4}-3x+1$ by finding all stationary points and testing their nature.

Also, find the points of inflection and the $y$ intercept.

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned} y&=\dfrac{x^3}{6}+\dfrac{x^2}{4}-3x+1\\ y'&=\dfrac{3x^2}{6}+\dfrac{2x}{4}-3 \end{aligned}$$
Stationary points occur when $y'=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 0&=\dfrac{x^2}{2}+\dfrac{x}{2}-3\\ &=\dfrac{1}{2}(x^2+x-6)\\ &=\dfrac{1}{2}(x+3)(x-2) \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} x=-3&: &y&=\dfrac{-27}{6}+\dfrac{9}{4}+9+1=\dfrac{31}{4}=7\dfrac{3}{4}\\ x=2&: &y&=\dfrac{8}{6}+\dfrac{4}{4}-6+1=-\dfrac{8}{3}=-2\dfrac{2}{3} \end{aligned}$$
Testing the nature with $y''=x+\dfrac{1}{2}$:
$$\begin{aligned} x&=-3: &y''&=-3+\dfrac{1}{2}=-2\dfrac{1}{2}<0 &&\text{maximum turning point at } \left(-3,\,7\dfrac{3}{4}\right)\\ x&=2: &y''&=2+\dfrac{1}{2}=2\dfrac{1}{2}>0 &&\text{minimum turning point at } \left(2,\,-2\dfrac{2}{3}\right) \end{aligned}$$
Possible points of inflexion occur when $y''=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} x+\dfrac{1}{2}&=0\\ x&=-\dfrac{1}{2} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} y&=\dfrac{-1}{8\times 6}+\dfrac{1}{4\times 4}-3\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right)+1\\ &=-\dfrac{1}{48}+\dfrac{1}{16}+\dfrac{3}{2}+1\\ &=\dfrac{61}{24}=2\dfrac{13}{24}\approx 2.5416 \end{aligned}$$
Testing the concavity either side:

\extable{Ts1250_1}

There is a change in concavity, $\therefore$ there is a point of inflexion at $\left(-\dfrac{1}{2},\,2\dfrac{13}{24}\right)$.

The $y$-intercept occurs when $x=0$: $y=0+0-0+1=1$.

parts.latex:
The curve $y=2x^3-ax^2+6x$ has a point of inflection at $x=4$.

What is the value of $a$?

solutions.latex:
At a point of inflection $y''=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} y&=2x^3-ax^2+6x\\ y'&=6x^2-2ax+6\\ y''&=12x-2a \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Show that there is a horizontal asymptote at $y=2$.

solutions.latex:
The horizontal asymptote is at $y=\displaystyle\lim_{x\to\infty}f(x)$. Dividing the numerator and denominator by $x^2$:
$$\begin{aligned} y&=\lim_{x\to\infty}f(x)\\ &=\lim_{x\to\infty}\dfrac{2x^2}{x^2-4}\\ &=\lim_{x\to\infty}\dfrac{\frac{2x^2}{x^2}}{\frac{x^2}{x^2}-\frac{4}{x^2}}\\ &=\lim_{x\to\infty}\dfrac{2}{1-\frac{4}{x^2}}\\ &=\dfrac{2}{1-0}\\ &=2 \end{aligned}$$

It is given that the shaded area shown above, bounded by the curve $f(t)=(t-1)^2e^{-t},\ 0\le t\le a$ and the $x$-axis is $1-\dfrac{2}{e}\text{ unit}^2$. \textit{(Do not prove this).}

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned}u&=(t-1)^2 & v&=e^{-t}\\ u'&=2(t-1) & v'&=-e^{-t}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}f'(t)&=2e^{-t}(t-1)-e^{-t}(t-1)^2\\ &=e^{-t}(t-1)(3-t)\end{aligned}$$
Stationary points occur where $f'(t)=0$; since $e^{-t}>0$:
$$t=1\text{ or } t=3$$
$$\begin{aligned}f(1)&=0\\ f(3)&=4e^{-3}\end{aligned}$$
As $t\to\infty$, $f(t)\to 0$ (the exponential dominates), so the $t$-axis is an asymptote.

solutions.latex:
Expanding:
$$f'(x)=3(x^2+2x-3)=3x^2+6x-9$$
Integrating:
$$\begin{aligned} f(x)&=\int\left(3x^2+6x-9\right)dx\\ &=x^3+3x^2-9x+C \end{aligned}$$
Apply the condition $f(2)=-8$ to find $C$:
$$\begin{aligned} -8&=(2)^3+3(2)^2-9(2)+C\\ -8&=2+C\\ C&=-10 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore f(x)=x^3+3x^2-9x-10$$

The maximum and minimum values on $-4\le x\le4$ occur at the endpoints or at the stationary points $x=-3$ and $x=1$ (where $f'(x)=0$).
$$\begin{aligned} f(-4)&=10 &&\text{endpoint}\\ f(4)&=66 &&\text{endpoint}\\ f(-3)&=17 &&\text{stationary point}\\ f(1)&=-15 &&\text{stationary point} \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ The minimum value is $-15$ and the maximum value is 66.

$$\begin{aligned} f'(x)&=3x^2+6x-9\\ f''(x)&=6x+6 \end{aligned}$$

Testing for a change in sign of $f''(x)$ around $x=-1$:
$$\begin{aligned} f''(-2)&=-6<0 &&\text{concave down}\\ f''(0)&=6>0 &&\text{concave up} \end{aligned}$$
The concavity changes, hence a point of inflection exists at $x=-1$.
$$f(-1)=-1+3+9-10=1$$
$\therefore$ The point of inflection is at $(-1,1)$.

solutions.latex:
For stationary points, $f'(x)=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 3x^2-4x+1&=0\\ (3x-1)(x-1)&=0\\ x&=\dfrac{1}{3},\ 1 \end{aligned}$$
For the nature of the stationary points, consider the sign of $f''(x)$.
$$f''(x)=6x-4$$
$$\begin{aligned} f''\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right)&=6\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right)-4=-2<0 &&\text{maximum turning point at } x=\dfrac{1}{3}\\ f''(1)&=6(1)-4=2>0 &&\text{minimum turning point at } x=1 \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore f(x)=x^3-2x^2+x-2$$

$$\begin{aligned} f(x)&=x^3-2x^2+x-2\\ &=x^2(x-2)+1(x-2)\\ &=\left(x^2+1\right)(x-2) \end{aligned}$$

The $y$-values of the stationary points:
$$\begin{aligned} f\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right)&=\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right)^3-2\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right)-2\\ &=-\dfrac{50}{27} \end{aligned}$$

solutions.latex:
Stationary points occur where $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=0$:
$$\dfrac{x(2-x)}{e^x}=0$$
$e^x>0$, so $x=0$ or $x=2$.

When $x=0$, $y=0$; when $x=2$, $y=4e^{-2}$.

At $(0,0)$:
$$\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=\dfrac{2}{1}=2>0$$
so the curve is concave up and $(0,0)$ is a local minimum.

At $(2,4e^{-2})$:
$$\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=\dfrac{4-8+2}{e^2}=-\dfrac{2}{e^2}<0$$
so the curve is concave down and $(2,4e^{-2})$ is a local maximum.

solutions.latex:
$f(x)$ is concave up where $f''(x)>0$.
$$\begin{aligned}f(x)&=-2x^3+k^3x^2\\f'(x)&=-6x^2+2k^3x\\f''(x)&=-12x+2k^3\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}-12x+2k^3&>0\\-12x&>-2k^3\\6x&<k^3\\x&<\dfrac{k^3}{6}\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ concave up for $x\in\left(-\infty,\dfrac{k^3}{6}\right)$.

Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=4x-1 & v&=e^{-\frac{x}{2}}\\ u'&=4 & v'&=-\dfrac{1}{2}e^{-\frac{x}{2}}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}y'&=4e^{-\frac{x}{2}}-\dfrac{1}{2}e^{-\frac{x}{2}}(4x-1)\\&=e^{-\frac{x}{2}}\left(4-\dfrac{1}{2}(4x-1)\right)\\&=e^{-\frac{x}{2}}\left(4-2x+\dfrac{1}{2}\right)\\&=e^{-\frac{x}{2}}\left(\dfrac{9}{2}-2x\right)\end{aligned}$$
Stationary points occur where $y'=0$. $e^{-\frac{x}{2}}\ne 0$, so
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{9}{2}-2x&=0\\x&=\dfrac{9}{4}\end{aligned}$$
When $x=\dfrac{9}{4}$, $y=8e^{-\frac{9}{8}}$, so the stationary point is $\left(\dfrac{9}{4},8e^{-\frac{9}{8}}\right)$.

Testing the sign of $y'$ either side ($e^{-\frac{x}{2}}>0$, so the sign is that of $\dfrac{9}{2}-2x$):

\extable{Ts1575_1}

$\therefore$ maximum turning point at $\left(\dfrac{9}{4},8e^{-\frac{9}{8}}\right)$.

parts.latex: If $y=\dfrac{\cos x}{1+\sin x}$, show that $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}+y\dfrac{dy}{dx}=0$.

Chain rule.reason: Second derivative of -1/(1+sin x) can equally be done by the quotient rule (agreed); method is free.

solutions.latex:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned}u&=\cos x & v&=1+\sin x\\u'&=-\sin x & v'&=\cos x\end{aligned}$$
Simplifying with $\sin^2x+\cos^2x=1$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dy}{dx}&=\dfrac{(1+\sin x)(-\sin x)-\cos x(\cos x)}{(1+\sin x)^2}\\&=\dfrac{-\sin x-\sin^2x-\cos^2x}{(1+\sin x)^2}\\&=\dfrac{-(1+\sin x)}{(1+\sin x)^2}\\&=\dfrac{-1}{1+\sin x}\end{aligned}$$
Writing $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=-(1+\sin x)^{-1}$ and using the chain rule:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}&=-(-(1+\sin x)^{-2})\cdot(\cos x)\\&=\dfrac{\cos x}{(1+\sin x)^2}\end{aligned}$$
Substituting into the left-hand side:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}+y\dfrac{dy}{dx}&=\dfrac{\cos x}{(1+\sin x)^2}+\dfrac{\cos x}{1+\sin x}\cdot\dfrac{-1}{1+\sin x}\\&=\dfrac{\cos x-\cos x}{(1+\sin x)^2}\\&=0\end{aligned}$$
as required.

solutions.latex:
Differentiating (chain rule):
$$\begin{aligned}y&=\sin\left(2x+\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)\\\dfrac{dy}{dx}&=2\cos\left(2x+\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)\end{aligned}$$
Stationary points occur where $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=0$. For $0\le x\le\pi$, $2x+\dfrac{\pi}{3}$ lies between $\dfrac{\pi}{3}$ and $\dfrac{7\pi}{3}$:
$$\begin{aligned}2\cos\left(2x+\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)&=0\\\cos\left(2x+\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)&=0\\2x+\dfrac{\pi}{3}&=\dfrac{\pi}{2},\dfrac{3\pi}{2}\\2x&=\dfrac{\pi}{6},\dfrac{7\pi}{6}\\x&=\dfrac{\pi}{12},\dfrac{7\pi}{12}\end{aligned}$$
When $x=\dfrac{\pi}{12}$,
$$y=\sin\left(2\times\dfrac{\pi}{12}+\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)=1$$
When $x=\dfrac{7\pi}{12}$,
$$y=\sin\left(2\times\dfrac{7\pi}{12}+\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)=-1$$
Testing the nature with the second derivative:
$$\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=-4\sin\left(2x+\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)$$
$$\begin{aligned}x&=\dfrac{\pi}{12}: &\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}&=-4\sin\left(2\times\dfrac{\pi}{12}+\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)=-4<0 &&\text{maximum}\\x&=\dfrac{7\pi}{12}: &\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}&=-4\sin\left(2\times\dfrac{7\pi}{12}+\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)=4>0 &&\text{minimum}\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore\left(\dfrac{\pi}{12},1\right)$ is a relative maximum turning point and $\left(\dfrac{7\pi}{12},-1\right)$ is a relative minimum turning point.
criteria: Finds the $y$ values of the stationary points, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Points of inflection can occur where $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}&=-4\sin\left(2x+\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)\\-4\sin\left(2x+\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)&=0\\\sin\left(2x+\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)&=0\\2x+\dfrac{\pi}{3}&=0,\pi,2\pi\end{aligned}$$
For $0\le x\le\pi$, $2x+\dfrac{\pi}{3}\ge\dfrac{\pi}{3}$, so $0$ is rejected:
$$\begin{aligned}2x&=\pi-\dfrac{\pi}{3}\text{ or }2\pi-\dfrac{\pi}{3}\\2x&=\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\text{ or }\dfrac{5\pi}{3}\\x&=\dfrac{2\pi}{6}\left(=\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)\text{ or }\dfrac{5\pi}{6}\end{aligned}$$
$\sin\theta$ changes sign at $\theta=\pi$ and $\theta=2\pi$, so $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}$ changes sign at both values: the concavity changes.

When $x=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$,
$$y=\sin\left(2\times\dfrac{\pi}{3}+\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)=0$$
When $x=\dfrac{5\pi}{6}$,
$$y=\sin\left(2\times\dfrac{5\pi}{6}+\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)=0$$
$\therefore$ Points of inflection are $\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3},0\right)$ and $\left(\dfrac{5\pi}{6},0\right)$

parts.latex: Sketch the curve $y=(x+1)e^{1-x}$ showing all important features including finding and classifying stationary points, points of inflection, intercepts and showing what happens to the curve as $x\to\pm\infty$.

solutions.latex:
$y$-intercept: when $x=0$, $y=e^{1}=e$.

$x$-intercept: $e^{1-x}\ne0$, so $(x+1)e^{1-x}=0$ gives $x+1=0$, that is $x=-1$.

Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned}u&=x+1 & v&=e^{1-x}\\ u'&=1 & v'&=-e^{1-x}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dy}{dx}&=e^{1-x}+(x+1)e^{1-x}\times(-1)\\ &=e^{1-x}(1-x-1)\\ &=-xe^{1-x}\end{aligned}$$
Stationary points where $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=0$: $x=0$, $y=e$.

Product rule again, with
$$\begin{aligned}u&=-x & v&=e^{1-x}\\ u'&=-1 & v'&=-e^{1-x}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}&=-1\times e^{1-x}-x\times e^{1-x}\times(-1)\\ &=e^{1-x}(-1+x)\end{aligned}$$
When $x=0$: $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=-1\times e^{1}<0$, concave down.

$\therefore (0,e)$ is a local maximum turning point.

Points of inflection are possible where $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=0$: $x=1$, $y=2\times e^{0}=2$, that is $(1,2)$.

\extable{Ts2103_1}

The concavity changes, so $(1,2)$ is a point of inflection.

Behaviour as $x\to\pm\infty$:
$$\begin{aligned}&x\to+\infty: && x+1\to+\infty,\ e^{1-x}\to0 && \therefore y\to0\\ &x\to-\infty: && x+1\to-\infty,\ e^{1-x}\to\infty && \therefore y\to-\infty\end{aligned}$$

Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with

$$\begin{aligned} u &= x^2 & v &= x-2 \\ u' &= 2x & v' &= 1 \end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} y' &= \dfrac{2x(x-2)-x^2(1)}{(x-2)^2} \\ &= \dfrac{2x^2-4x-x^2}{(x-2)^2} \\ &= \dfrac{x^2-4x}{(x-2)^2} \\ &= \dfrac{x(x-4)}{(x-2)^2} \end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} x=0: &\quad y=0 \\ x=4: &\quad y=8 \end{aligned}$$

The denominator $(x-2)^2$ is positive, so the sign of $y'$ is the sign of $x(x-4)$. Testing the nature:

\exfigure{339_q16_s1}

Hence $(0,0)$ is a maximum turning point and $(4,8)$ is a minimum turning point.

parts.latex:
Which of the following statements is \textbf{true} for the function

$$f(x)=\dfrac{2}{3}x^3-6x^2+20x-5?$$

Increasing and decreasing functions.evidence: f'(x)>0 for all x. Hence f(x) is increasing for all x

Stationary points and their nature.evidence: For stationary points, f'(x)=0 ... no maximum or minimum

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned}f(x)&=\dfrac{2}{3}x^3-6x^2+20x-5\\f'(x)&=2x^2-12x+20\\f''(x)&=4x-12\end{aligned}$$
For stationary points, $f'(x)=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}2x^2-12x+20&=0\\x^2-6x+10&=0\end{aligned}$$
$$\Delta=(-6)^2-4(1)(10)=-4<0$$
There are no solutions, and $f'(x)$ is a parabola with $a=2>0$, so $f'(x)>0$ for all $x$.

Hence $f(x)$ is increasing for all $x$ and has no maximum or minimum.

For a point of inflection, $f''(x)=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}4x-12&=0\\x&=3\end{aligned}$$
Test the concavity either side of $x=3$:
$$\begin{aligned}f''(2)&=4(2)-12=-4<0 &&\text{concave down}\\f''(4)&=4(4)-12=4>0 &&\text{concave up}\end{aligned}$$
The concavity changes at $x=3$, so $f(x)$ has a point of inflection.

solutions.latex:
Concave up means $y''>0$.
$$\begin{aligned}y'&=4x^3-48x+2 \\ y''&=12x^2-48\end{aligned}$$
Solve $y''>0$:
$$\begin{aligned}12x^2-48&>0 \\ 12(x-2)(x+2)&>0\end{aligned}$$
This is an upward parabola in $x$, so it is positive outside its roots $x=\pm 2$.
$$\therefore\ x<-2\ \text{ or }\ x>2$$

solutions.latex:
Differentiate $f'(x)=3e^x\left(3x^2+x^3\right)$ using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned}u&=3e^x & v&=3x^2+x^3 \\ u'&=3e^x & v'&=6x+3x^2\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}f''(x)&=3e^x\left(3x^2+x^3\right)+3e^x\left(6x+3x^2\right) \\ &=9x^2e^x+3x^3e^x+18xe^x+9x^2e^x \\ &=18xe^x+18x^2e^x+3x^3e^x \\ &=3xe^x\left(6+6x+x^2\right)\end{aligned}$$
Possible points of inflection: $f''(x)=0$, so $3xe^x\left(x^2+6x+6\right)=0$. Since $e^x>0$, either $x=0$ or $x^2+6x+6=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}x&=\dfrac{-6\pm\sqrt{36-4(1)(6)}}{2} \\ &=\dfrac{-6\pm\sqrt{12}}{2} \\ &=-3\pm\sqrt{3} \\ &\approx -1.3,\ -4.7 &&(\text{to 1 dp})\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}f(0)&=3(0)^3e^0=0 \\ f\left(-3+\sqrt{3}\right)&\approx -1.7 \\ f\left(-3-\sqrt{3}\right)&\approx -2.8\end{aligned}$$
Test whether the concavity changes (use $f''(x)$, not gradients):

\extable{Ts2797_1}

$f''(x)$ changes sign at each of the three values of $x$: from $<0$ to $>0$ about $x=-4.7$, from $>0$ to $<0$ about $x=-1.3$, and from $<0$ to $>0$ about $x=0$.
$$\therefore\ \text{points of inflection } (0,0),\ (-1.3,-1.7)\text{ and }(-4.7,-2.8)$$

solutions.latex:
$$y=1-e^{-x^2}$$
Using the chain rule,
$$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=2xe^{-x^2}$$
Stationary points: $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=0$. Since $e^{-x^2}>0$, this needs $2x=0$, so $x=0$ and $y=1-e^{0}=0$.

For the nature, use the second derivative (product rule with $u=2x$, $v=e^{-x^2}$):
$$\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=2e^{-x^2}-4x^2e^{-x^2}=e^{-x^2}\left(2-4x^2\right)$$
At $x=0$, $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=2>0$, so $(0,0)$ is a minimum turning point.
criteria: Finds $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ and the stationary point, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
From part (a),
$$\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=e^{-x^2}\left(2-4x^2\right)$$
Possible inflections: $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=0$. Since $e^{-x^2}>0$,
$$\begin{aligned} 2-4x^2 &= 0 \\ x^2 &= \dfrac{1}{2} \\ x &= \pm\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \end{aligned}$$
Test for a change in concavity (the sign of $2-4x^2$ decides the sign):
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} &< 0 &&\text{for } x<-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} &&\text{concave down}\\ \dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} &> 0 &&\text{for } -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}<x<\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} &&\text{concave up}\\ \dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} &< 0 &&\text{for } x>\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} &&\text{concave down} \end{aligned}$$
The concavity changes at both values, so there are points of inflection at $x=\pm\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$.

parts.latex: Show that the curve $y=3x^2-5\ln x$ is concave up for all values of $x>0$.

solutions.latex:
Concave up means $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}>0$.
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dy}{dx}&=6x-\dfrac{5}{x} \\ \dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}&=6+\dfrac{5}{x^2}\end{aligned}$$
For $x>0$, $x^2>0$, so $\dfrac{5}{x^2}>0$ and $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=6+\dfrac{5}{x^2}>0$.

$\therefore$ the curve is concave up for all $x>0$.

parts.latex: Sketch the graph of the curve $y=\dfrac{5x^2e^{\frac{x}{2}}}{3}$ showing the coordinates of the turning points and their nature.

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=\dfrac{5x^2}{3} & v&=e^{\frac{x}{2}}\\ u'&=\dfrac{10x}{3} & v'&=\dfrac{1}{2}e^{\frac{x}{2}}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}y'&=\dfrac{10x}{3}e^{\frac{x}{2}}+\dfrac{5x^2}{3}\cdot\dfrac{1}{2}e^{\frac{x}{2}}\\ &=\dfrac{5x}{3}e^{\frac{x}{2}}\left(2+\dfrac{x}{2}\right)\end{aligned}$$
For stationary points $y'=0$. Since $e^{\frac{x}{2}}\ne0$, either $\dfrac{5x}{3}=0$ or $2+\dfrac{x}{2}=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}x&=0, & y&=0\\ x&=-4, & y&=\dfrac{5.16}{3}e^{-2}=\dfrac{80}{3e^2}\end{aligned}$$
Test the sign of $y'$ either side of each point:
$$\begin{aligned}x=-5:&\quad y'\approx0.34>0\\ x=-4:&\quad y'=0\\ x=-1:&\quad y'\approx-1.5<0\end{aligned}$$
so $\left(-4,\dfrac{80}{3e^2}\right)$ is a maximum turning point.
$$\begin{aligned}x=-1:&\quad y'\approx-1.5<0\\ x=0:&\quad y'=0\\ x=1:&\quad y'\approx6.9>0\end{aligned}$$
so $(0,0)$ is a minimum turning point.

As $x\to-\infty$, $y\to0^{+}$, so the $x$-axis is a horizontal asymptote.

$$\begin{aligned}12x^3-12x^2&=0\\ 12x^2(x-1)&=0\end{aligned}$$
so $x=0$ or $x=1$.

At $x=1$: $y=3-4+2=1$ and $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=36-24=12>0$, so $(1,1)$ is a minimum turning point.

At $x=0$: $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=0$, so the second derivative test fails and the concavity is tested below.

For points of inflexion, $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}36x^2-24x&=0\\ 12x(3x-2)&=0\end{aligned}$$
so $x=0$ or $x=\dfrac{2}{3}$. When $x=\dfrac{2}{3}$, $y=3\left(\dfrac{2}{3}\right)^4-4\left(\dfrac{2}{3}\right)^3+2=\dfrac{38}{27}$.

Test the concavity either side of each value:

\extable{Ts2888_1}

The concavity changes at both values. At $x=0$ the gradient is also $0$, so $(0,2)$ is a horizontal point of inflexion, not a turning point. $\left(\dfrac{2}{3},\dfrac{38}{27}\right)$ is also a point of inflexion.

The $y$-intercept is $(0,2)$.

parts.latex:
The displacement of a particle is given by the equation below, where $t$ is the time in seconds for $0\le t\le 9$

$$x=\dfrac{t^3}{3}-4t^2+12t-2$$

Find the time(s) when the particle is at rest.

For the function $f(x)=\dfrac{1+x}{e^{x}}$, $f(x)\to 0$ as $x\to\infty$ .

Sketch $y=f(x)$ showing all key features including any stationary points and points of inflexion.

solutions.latex:
The particle is at rest when $v=\dfrac{dx}{dt}=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}v&=t^2-8t+12\\ t^2-8t+12&=0\\ (t-2)(t-6)&=0\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ t=2\text{ s or }t=6\text{ s}$$

\exfigure{995_q15_s1}

$f(x)=e^{-x}(1+x)$. Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=e^{-x} & v&=1+x\\ u'&=-e^{-x} & v'&=1\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}f'(x)&=-e^{-x}(1+x)+e^{-x}\\ &=e^{-x}\left(1-(1+x)\right)\\ &=-xe^{-x}\end{aligned}$$
For stationary points, $f'(x)=0$: $-xe^{-x}=0$ gives $x=0$, since $e^{-x}\ne0$. Then $f(0)=\dfrac{1+0}{e^0}=1$, giving $(0,1)$.

To find the nature, differentiate $f'(x)=-xe^{-x}$ with the product rule, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=-x & v&=e^{-x}\\ u'&=-1 & v'&=-e^{-x}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}f''(x)&=-e^{-x}+(-x)\left(-e^{-x}\right)\\ &=e^{-x}(x-1)\end{aligned}$$
$f''(0)=e^0(-1)=-1<0$, so $(0,1)$ is a local maximum.

For points of inflexion, $f''(x)=0$: $e^{-x}(x-1)=0$ gives $x=1$, since $e^{-x}\ne0$. Then $f(1)=\dfrac{2}{e}$. Test the concavity either side:

\extable{Ts2928_1}

$f''(0)=-1<0$ and $f''(2)=e^{-2}(2-1)=\dfrac{1}{e^2}>0$, so the concavity changes and $\left(1,\dfrac{2}{e}\right)$ is a point of inflexion.

As $x\to\infty$, $f(x)\to0$, so the $x$-axis is a horizontal asymptote.

parts.latex:
The function $y=f(x)$ is defined as

$$f(x)=\begin{cases}1 & \text{for } -3\le x\le 0\\ -x^2+1 & \text{for } x>0\end{cases}$$

Determine whether $y=f(x)$ is both continuous $\textbf{and}$ differentiable at $x=0$.

Justify your answer with appropriate calculations.

solutions.latex:
Check continuity at $x=0$: both pieces must give the same value.
$$\begin{aligned}\text{left: } f(0)&=1\\\text{right: } -0^2+1&=1\end{aligned}$$
So $f$ is continuous at $x=0$.

Check the gradients from each side. Each piece is differentiable for all real $x$ on its own.
$$\begin{aligned}\text{left: } f'(x)&=0\\\text{right: } y&=-x^2+1\\y'&=-2x,\ \text{so } y'(0)=0\end{aligned}$$
The gradients agree ($0=0$), so $f$ is differentiable at $x=0$.
$$\therefore\ f(x)\text{ is both continuous and differentiable at } x=0$$
criteria: Shows continuity at $x=0$ (both pieces give $1$), or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
Let $f(x)=x^4+x^3+kx^2-3x-5$, where $k$ is a constant.

Find the values of $k$ for which $f(x)$ is always concave up.

solutions.latex:
A function is concave up when $f''(x)>0$.
$$\begin{aligned}f'(x)&=4x^3+3x^2+2kx-3\\f''(x)&=12x^2+6x+2k\end{aligned}$$
$f''(x)>0$ for all $x$ requires the quadratic $2\left(6x^2+3x+k\right)$ to have positive leading coefficient ($6>0$) and $\Delta<0$.
$$\begin{aligned}3^2-4\times 6\times k&<0\\9-24k&<0\\k&>\dfrac{3}{8}\end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: By showing that $f'(x)=3\left(1-\dfrac{x}{4}\right)^2(1-x)$, find any stationary points and determine their nature.
Explain why the graph of $y=f(x)$ must cross the $x$-axis at least once between $x=5$ and $x=6$.

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u &= 3x & v &= \left(1-\dfrac{x}{4}\right)^3 \\ u' &= 3 & v' &= -\dfrac{3}{4}\left(1-\dfrac{x}{4}\right)^2 \end{aligned}$$
where $v'$ comes from the chain rule.
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x) &= 3\left(1-\dfrac{x}{4}\right)^3-\dfrac{9x}{4}\left(1-\dfrac{x}{4}\right)^2 \\ &= 3\left(1-\dfrac{x}{4}\right)^2\left[\left(1-\dfrac{x}{4}\right)-\dfrac{3x}{4}\right] \\ &= 3\left(1-\dfrac{x}{4}\right)^2(1-x) \end{aligned}$$
For stationary points $f'(x)=0$, so $x=4$ or $x=1$.
$$\begin{aligned} f(1) &= 3\left(\dfrac{3}{4}\right)^3+1 = 2\dfrac{17}{64} \\ f(4) &= 1 \end{aligned}$$
The stationary points are $\left(1,2\dfrac{17}{64}\right)$ and $(4,1)$.

Nature of $x=1$: the factor $(1-x)$ decides the sign of $f'$ near $x=1$.
$$\begin{aligned} f'(0) &= 3>0 \\ f'(2) &= -\dfrac{3}{4}<0 \end{aligned}$$
$f'$ changes from positive to negative, so $\left(1,2\dfrac{17}{64}\right)$ is a local maximum.

Nature of $x=4$: the squared factor does not change sign.
$$\begin{aligned} f'(3) &= -\dfrac{3}{8}<0 \\ f'(5) &= -\dfrac{3}{4}<0 \end{aligned}$$
$f'$ is negative on both sides of $x=4$, so $(4,1)$ is a horizontal point of inflexion.

Stationary points occur where $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=0$.

$$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=6x^2-12x=6x(x-2)=0$$

So $x=0$ or $x=2$.

A table of values of $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ either side of each point is an equivalent justification.

$$\therefore\ (0,0)\text{ is a maximum and }(2,-8)\text{ is a minimum}$$

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x & v&=(x+1)^3\\ u'&=1 & v'&=3(x+1)^2\end{aligned}$$

The concavity changes at both $x=0$ and $x=1$.

The function $f(x)$ is defined for $a \le x \le b$. On this interval $f'(x) > 0$ and $f''(x) < 0$.

solutions.latex:
Since $f'(x)>0$, the graph is increasing on $a\le x\le b$ (gradient positive).

Since $f''(x)<0$, the gradient is decreasing, so the graph is concave down: it rises, getting less steep.

Options C and D are decreasing, so they fail $f'(x)>0$.

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=4x & v&=e^{-x}\\ u'&=4 & v'&=-e^{-x}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dy}{dx} &= 4e^{-x}-4xe^{-x} \\ &= 4e^{-x}(1-x) \end{aligned}$$
Stationary points occur where $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=0$. Since $e^{-x}>0$, $x=1$, and $y=4e^{-1}$.

To find the nature, use the second derivative:
$$\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=-4e^{-x}(2-x)$$
At $x=1$,
$$\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=-4e^{-1}<0$$
$$\therefore\ (1,4e^{-1})\text{ is a maximum turning point}$$

A point of inflection needs $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=0$:

$$\begin{aligned} x=1.9:\ & \dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}<0 &&\text{concave down}\\ x=2.1:\ & \dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}>0 &&\text{concave up}\end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Sketch the curve $y=x^2e^x$ showing all important features including finding and classifying stationary points, inflections, intercepts and show what happens to the curve as $x\to\pm\infty$.

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with

$$\begin{aligned} u&=x^2 & v&=e^x \\ u'&=2x & v'&=e^x \end{aligned}$$

$$y'=2xe^x+x^2e^x=xe^x(2+x)$$

Differentiating again (product rule on each term):

$$y''=e^x(2+4x+x^2)$$

Stationary points: $y'=0$. Since $e^x\ne0$, either $x=0$ or $2+x=0$, so $x=0$ or $x=-2$.

When $x=0$, $y=0$. When $x=-2$, $y=\dfrac{4}{e^2}$.

Nature, using the sign of $y''$:

$$\begin{aligned} x=0:\ y''&=1(2)>0 &&\text{minimum at }(0,0) \\ x=-2:\ y''&=e^{-2}(2-8+4)<0 &&\text{maximum at }\left(-2,\dfrac{4}{e^2}\right) \end{aligned}$$

Inflections: $y''=0$. Since $e^x\ne0$,

$$\begin{aligned} x^2+4x+2&=0 \\ x&=\dfrac{-4\pm\sqrt{16-8}}{2} \\ &=-2\pm\sqrt{2} \end{aligned}$$

Test the concavity either side of each root, using the sign of $x^2+4x+2$:

$$\begin{aligned} x=-4,\ -3.4,\ -1 &&&\text{signs of }y''\text{: }>0,\ 0,\ <0 \\ x=-1,\ -0.6,\ 0 &&&\text{signs of }y''\text{: }<0,\ 0,\ >0 \end{aligned}$$

The concavity changes at both roots, so both are points of inflection.

As $x\to-\infty$, $y\to0^+$ (the exponential dominates), and as $x\to\infty$, $y\to\infty$.

\exfigure{1544_q32_s1}

solutions.latex:
Turning points occur where $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=0$.
$$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=-3x^{2}+2x+1$$
$$\begin{aligned} 3x^{2}-2x-1&=0 \\ (3x+1)(x-1)&=0 \end{aligned}$$
So $x=-\dfrac{1}{3}$ or $x=1$.

When $x=-\dfrac{1}{3}$:
$$\begin{aligned} y&=-\left(-\dfrac{1}{3}\right)^{3}+\left(-\dfrac{1}{3}\right)^{2}+\left(-\dfrac{1}{3}\right)+3 \\ &=2\dfrac{22}{27} \end{aligned}$$
When $x=1$:
$$\begin{aligned} y&=-1+1+1+3 \\ &=4 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ A\left(-\dfrac{1}{3},2\dfrac{22}{27}\right),\ B(1,4)$$
criteria: Finds the derivative, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The curve is concave down when $\dfrac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}<0$.
$$\dfrac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}=-6x+2$$
$$\begin{aligned} -6x+2&<0 \\ 6x&>2 \\ x&>\dfrac{1}{3} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the curve is concave down for } x>\dfrac{1}{3}$$
criteria: Finds the second derivative $-6x+2$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
One real solution means the line $y=k$ meets the curve only once.

This happens when $y=k$ lies above the maximum turning point $y=4$ or below the minimum turning point $y=2\dfrac{22}{27}$.
$$\therefore\ k>4 \text{ or } k<2\dfrac{22}{27}$$

parts.latex: Find all the stationary points on the curve in the given domain.
By finding the second derivative or otherwise, determine the nature of stationary points.
Find the $x-$values of points of inflexion, correct to 1 decimal place.

On the given axes, draw the graph of $y = e^{\sin x}$, showing all the information obtained in parts (a) to (c).

\exfigure{570_q26_1}

solutions.latex:
Differentiate using the chain rule:
$$y' = e^{\sin x}\cos x$$
Set $y'=0$. Since $e^{\sin x} > 0$, we need $\cos x = 0$, so
$$x = \dfrac{\pi}{2},\ \dfrac{3\pi}{2}$$
The $y$ values are
$$f\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) = e^{1} = e, \qquad f\left(\dfrac{3\pi}{2}\right) = e^{-1} = \dfrac{1}{e}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{stationary points } \left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}, e\right) \text{ and } \left(\dfrac{3\pi}{2}, \dfrac{1}{e}\right)$$
criteria: Obtains one correct stationary point or $x = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$ or $\dfrac{3\pi}{2}$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Differentiate $y'=e^{\sin x}\cos x$ using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=e^{\sin x} & v&=\cos x\\ u'&=e^{\sin x}\cos x & v'&=-\sin x\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} y'' &= e^{\sin x}\cos^2 x - e^{\sin x}\sin x \\ &= e^{\sin x}\left(\cos^2 x - \sin x\right) \end{aligned}$$
Note $e^{\sin x} > 0$.

At $x=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$:
$$y'' = e^{1}(0 - 1) = -e < 0$$
so a maximum at $\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}, e\right)$.

At $x=\dfrac{3\pi}{2}$:
$$y'' = e^{-1}(0 + 1) = e^{-1} > 0$$
so a minimum at $\left(\dfrac{3\pi}{2}, \dfrac{1}{e}\right)$.
criteria: Correctly checks the nature of both stationary points, or equivalent merit
Correct second derivative, or correctly checks the nature of one stationary point, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Points of inflexion occur where $y''=0$:
$$e^{\sin x}\left(\cos^2 x - \sin x\right) = 0$$
Since $e^{\sin x} > 0$, $\cos^2 x - \sin x = 0$. Using $\cos^2 x = 1-\sin^2 x$:
$$\begin{aligned} 1 - \sin^2 x - \sin x &= 0 \\ \sin^2 x + \sin x - 1 &= 0 \\ \sin x &= \dfrac{-1 \pm \sqrt{5}}{2} \end{aligned}$$
$\dfrac{-1-\sqrt{5}}{2}<-1$ has no solution, so $\sin x=\dfrac{\sqrt{5}-1}{2}$.

Hence $x \approx 0.7$ or $x \approx 2.5$ (radians). Concavity changes at both (checked with a table of $y''$ values), giving points of inflexion at about $(0.7, 1.9)$ and $(2.5, 1.9)$ (both have $y=e^{\sin x}=e^{0.618\ldots}\approx1.86$).

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned} f(x) &= x^3 - 3x^2 + 3 \\ f'(x) &= 3x^2 - 6x \\ f''(x) &= 6x - 6 \end{aligned}$$

Stationary points occur when $f'(x) = 0$.

$$\begin{aligned} 3x^2 - 6x &= 0 \\ 3x(x-2) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$

So $x = 0$ or $x = 2$, both in the domain $-1 \le x < 3$.

When $x = 0$, $y = 3$. When $x = 2$, $y = 8 - 12 + 3 = -1$.

The second derivative decides the nature:

$$\begin{aligned} f''(0) &= -6 < 0 &&\text{maximum turning point}\\ f''(2) &= 6 > 0 &&\text{minimum turning point}\end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ (0, 3) \text{ is a maximum and } (2, -1) \text{ is a minimum turning point}$$

2843.stem: Consider the curve given by $y=x^3-x^2-x+6$, for $-3\leq x\leq 3$.

figures.cap: solution sketch: sketch of the cubic curve with key points

parts.latex: Find the coordinates of the stationary points and determine their nature.
Show that there is a point of inflection at $\left(\dfrac{1}{3},\dfrac{151}{27}\right)$.
Sketch the curve for $-3\leq x\leq 3$, showing all key features.
For what values of $x$ is the curve decreasing and concaving up?

solutions.latex:
Stationary points occur where $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} y &= x^3-x^2-x+6 \\ \dfrac{dy}{dx} &= 3x^2-2x-1 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} 3x^2-2x-1 &= 0 \\ (3x+1)(x-1) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
So $x=-\dfrac{1}{3}$ or $x=1$, giving $y=\dfrac{167}{27}$ and $y=5$ respectively.

The second derivative decides the nature.
$$\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=6x-2$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{At } x=-\dfrac{1}{3}: \quad \dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} &= 6\times\left(-\dfrac{1}{3}\right)-2=-4<0 \\ \text{At } x=1: \quad \dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} &= 6\times 1-2=4>0 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \left(-\dfrac{1}{3},\dfrac{167}{27}\right) \text{ is a maximum turning point and } (1,5) \text{ is a minimum turning point}$$
criteria: Finds both stationary points, or equivalent merit
Finds the correct $x$ values for the turning points, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
A point of inflection needs $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=0$ with a change in concavity.
$$\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=6x-2$$
$$\begin{aligned} 6x-2 &= 0 \\ x &= \dfrac{1}{3} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} y &= \left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right)^3-\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right)^2-\dfrac{1}{3}+6 \\ &= \dfrac{151}{27} \end{aligned}$$
\extable{Ts4025_1}

There is a change in concavity, therefore the point of inflection is $\left(\dfrac{1}{3},\dfrac{151}{27}\right)$.

criteria: Correct curve with some key features shown, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The curve is decreasing for $\dfrac{dy}{dx}<0$, that is $-\dfrac{1}{3}<x<1$, and concave up for $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}>0$, that is $x>\dfrac{1}{3}$.

Both hold together when:
$$\therefore\ \dfrac{1}{3}<x<1$$

A curve is defined by $f(x)=\dfrac{1}{4}x^4-2x^2+1$.

The $y$-intercept is $f(0)=1$.

Stationary points: $f'(x)=0$.
$$f'(x)=x^3-4x=x(x^2-4)=0$$
So $x=0,\ \pm2$, giving $(0,1)$, $(2,-3)$ and $(-2,-3)$.

The concavity changes at both, so $\left(\pm\dfrac{2}{\sqrt3},-\dfrac{11}{9}\right)$ are points of inflection.

End points: $f(\pm3)=3.25$, so $(\pm3,3.25)$.

$$\therefore\ \text{the curve is concave down for } -\dfrac{2}{\sqrt3}<x<\dfrac{2}{\sqrt3}$$

parts.latex:
For the function $y = x^3 + \dfrac{3}{2}x^2 - 6x - 1$, find the stationary points and determine their nature and find any points of inflexion. Sketch the curve for $-4 \le x \le 2$.

solutions.latex:
Differentiate to find the stationary points.
$$\begin{aligned} y' &= 3x^2 + 3x - 6 \\ &= 3(x+2)(x-1) \end{aligned}$$
Stationary points occur when $y'=0$, so $x=-2$ or $x=1$.

When $x=-2$, $y=9$. When $x=1$, $y=-4.5$.

Nature: $y''=6x+3$ decides the sign.
$$\begin{aligned} y''(-2) &= -9 < 0 &&\text{so } (-2, 9) \text{ is a maximum turning point}\\ y''(1) &= 9 > 0 &&\text{so } (1, -4.5) \text{ is a minimum turning point} \end{aligned}$$
Inflexion: $y''=0$ when $x=-\dfrac{1}{2}$, giving $y=2\dfrac{1}{4}$.

Test the concavity either side:
$$\begin{aligned} y''(-1) &= -3 < 0 &&\text{concave down}\\ y''(0) &= 3 > 0 &&\text{concave up} \end{aligned}$$
The concavity changes, so $\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}, 2\dfrac{1}{4}\right)$ is a point of inflexion (not horizontal).

Endpoints of the domain: $(-4,-17)$ and $(2,1)$.

parts.latex:
Suppose $f(x) = 2x^2 - x - 1$ and $g(x) = \cos x$.

Find vertical asymptotes of $\dfrac{1}{f(g(x))}$ $\;(0 \le x \le \pi)$.

solutions.latex:
Substitute $g(x)=\cos x$ into $f$.
$$\dfrac{1}{f(g(x))} = \dfrac{1}{2\cos^2 x - \cos x - 1}$$
Vertical asymptotes occur where the denominator is zero, so $2\cos^2 x - \cos x - 1 = 0$.

Let $u=\cos x$.
$$\begin{aligned} 2u^2 - u - 1 &= 0 \\ (2u+1)(u-1) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
So $u=-\dfrac{1}{2}$ or $u=1$, that is $\cos x=-\dfrac{1}{2}$ or $\cos x=1$.

For $0\le x\le\pi$:
$$\therefore\ x=\dfrac{2\pi}{3} \text{ or } x=0$$

parts.latex:
For $f(x)$, a differentiable function, $f'(x) < 0$ and $f''(x) > 0$.

If $a$ and $b$ are in the domain of $f(x)$ and $a < b$, which statement is NOT always true?

solutions.latex:
$f'(x)<0$ means $f$ is decreasing, and $f''(x)>0$ means $f'$ is increasing, so the graph is decreasing and concave up.

Option A: decreasing, so $a<b$ gives $f(a)>f(b)$. Always true.

Option B says $f'(b)<f'(a)$. Since $f'$ is increasing, $a<b$ gives $f'(a)<f'(b)$, so this is false.

Option C: the gradient at $a$ is less than the gradient of the chord from $a$ to $b$ for a concave up curve. Always true.

Option D: the gradient at $b$ is greater than the gradient of the chord. Always true.

The statement that is not always true is option B.

parts.latex: Consider the function $f(x) = (x-2)^2(x+1)$
Find the two stationary points and determine their nature.
Sketch the graph of the function, clearly showing the stationary points and the $x$ and $y$ intercepts.

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=(x-2)^2 & v&=x+1\\ u'&=2(x-2) & v'&=1\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x) &= 2(x-2)(x+1) + (x-2)^2 \\ &= (x-2)(2x+2+x-2) \\ &= 3x(x-2) \end{aligned}$$
Differentiating again,
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x) &= 3x^2 - 6x \\ f''(x) &= 6x - 6 \end{aligned}$$
Stationary points occur where $f'(x) = 0$, so $x = 0$ or $x = 2$.

Test the second derivative at each point.

At $x = 2$: $f''(2) = 6 > 0$ and $f(2) = 0$, so there is a local minimum at $(2, 0)$.

At $x = 0$: $f''(0) = -6 < 0$ and $f(0) = 4$, so there is a local maximum at $(0, 4)$.

Alternatively, test the sign of $f'(x)$:
$$\begin{aligned} f'(-1) &= 9 &&\text{positive}\\ f'(1) &= -3 &&\text{negative}\\ f'(3) &= 9 &&\text{positive} \end{aligned}$$
The sign changes from positive to negative through $x = 0$ (local maximum), and from negative to positive through $x = 2$ (local minimum).

parts.latex: Show that the curve $y=x^2-8\ln x$ is concave up for all values of $x>0$.

solutions.latex:
Concave up needs $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}>0$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dy}{dx}&=2x-\dfrac{8}{x}\\ \dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}&=2+\dfrac{8}{x^2} \end{aligned}$$
For $x>0$, $\dfrac{8}{x^2}>0$, so $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}>2>0$.

Therefore the curve is concave up for all $x>0$.

parts.latex: Find the coordinates and nature of the stationary points on the curve $y=\dfrac{x^2}{x-2}$.

solutions.latex:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x^2 & v&=x-2\\ u'&=2x & v'&=1\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dy}{dx} &= \dfrac{2x(x-2)-x^2}{(x-2)^2} \\ &= \dfrac{x^2-4x}{(x-2)^2} \\ &= \dfrac{x(x-4)}{(x-2)^2} \end{aligned}$$
Stationary points occur where $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=0$, so $x=0$ or $x=4$.

When $x=0$, $y=0$. When $x=4$, $y=8$.

The stationary points are $(0,0)$ and $(4,8)$.

The denominator is positive except at $x=2$, so the sign of $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ is the sign of $x(x-4)$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dy}{dx} &> 0 &&\text{for } x<0 &&\text{increasing}\\ \dfrac{dy}{dx} &= 0 &&\text{at } x=0\\ \dfrac{dy}{dx} &< 0 &&\text{for } 0<x<2 &&\text{decreasing}\\ \dfrac{dy}{dx} &\text{ undefined} &&\text{at } x=2\\ \dfrac{dy}{dx} &< 0 &&\text{for } 2<x<4 &&\text{decreasing}\\ \dfrac{dy}{dx} &= 0 &&\text{at } x=4\\ \dfrac{dy}{dx} &> 0 &&\text{for } x>4 &&\text{increasing}\end{aligned}$$
Hence $(0,0)$ is a maximum turning point and $(4,8)$ is a minimum turning point.

parts.latex: Find the stationary points and determine their nature.
Find any points of inflexion.

solutions.latex:
Differentiate, then stationary points occur when $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=0$.
$$\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 12x - 3x^2$$
$$\begin{aligned} 0 &= 12x - 3x^2 \\ &= 3x(4-x) \end{aligned}$$
So $x = 0$ or $x = 4$.

When $x=0$, $y=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{When } x=4,\ y &= 6\times 4^2 - 4^3 \\ &= 32 \end{aligned}$$
\extable{Ts4660_1}

The slope is decreasing, flat, increasing, flat, decreasing, so there is a maximum turning point at $(4,32)$ and a minimum turning point at $(0,0)$.

Alternatively, use the second derivative.
$$\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} = 12 - 6x$$
At $x=0$, $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} = 12>0$ (concave up), so a minimum.

At $x=4$, $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} = -12<0$ (concave down), so a maximum.
$$\therefore\ \text{maximum at } (4,32),\ \text{minimum at } (0,0)$$

parts.latex: Find the stationary point on the curve $y=e^{x^{2}+4x}$ and determine its nature.

solutions.latex:
Differentiate using the chain rule.
$$y'=(2x+4)e^{x^{2}+4x}$$
Stationary points occur where $y'=0$. Since $e^{x^{2}+4x}>0$, we need $2x+4=0$, so $x=-2$.

Test the nature using the second derivative, using the product rule.
$$y''=2e^{x^{2}+4x}+(2x+4)^{2}e^{x^{2}+4x}$$
At $x=-2$:
$$y''=2e^{-4}>0$$
So the stationary point is a minimum. When $x=-2$, $y=e^{-4}$.
$$\therefore\ \text{minimum stationary point at } \left(-2,\,e^{-4}\right)$$

parts.latex: Find the $x$- and $y$-intercepts.

solutions.latex:
For the $x$-intercept, let $y = 0$:
$$0 = \dfrac{2x}{e^x}$$
so $2x = 0$, giving $x = 0$. The $x$-intercept is $(0,0)$.

For the $y$-intercept, let $x = 0$:
$$y = \dfrac{2(0)}{e^0} = 0$$
The $y$-intercept is $(0,0)$.

$$\therefore\ \text{the only intercept is at the origin}$$

Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=2x & v&=e^x\\ u'&=2 & v'&=e^x\end{aligned}$$
$$\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{(e^x)(2) - (2x)(e^x)}{(e^x)^2} = \dfrac{2e^x(1-x)}{e^{2x}} = \dfrac{2(1-x)}{e^x}$$
For stationary points, $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 0 &= \dfrac{2(1-x)}{e^x} \\ 1 - x &= 0 \\ x &= 1 \end{aligned}$$
When $x = 1$, $y = \dfrac{2}{e}$.

The sign of $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ either side of $x=1$ gives its nature:

\extable{Ts4729_1}

The gradient changes from positive to negative, so $\left(1, \dfrac{2}{e}\right)$ is a maximum turning point.
criteria: Finds the stationary point at $\left(1, \dfrac{2}{e}\right)$, or equivalent merit
Finds the derivative, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
From part (b), $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{2(1-x)}{e^x}$.

Using the quotient rule with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=1-x & v&=e^x\\ u'&=-1 & v'&=e^x\end{aligned}$$
$$\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} = 2\left[\dfrac{(e^x)(-1) - (1-x)(e^x)}{e^{2x}}\right] = 2\left(\dfrac{xe^x - 2e^x}{e^{2x}}\right) = \dfrac{2(x-2)}{e^x}$$
For a possible point of inflection, $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} = 0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 0 &= \dfrac{2(x-2)}{e^x} \\ x &= 2 \end{aligned}$$
When $x = 2$, $y = \dfrac{4}{e^2}$.

The sign of $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}$ either side of $x=2$ tests the concavity:

\extable{Ts4730_1}

The concavity changes, so $\left(2, \dfrac{4}{e^2}\right)$ is a point of inflection.

parts.latex: Find the $x$ coordinate(s) of the stationary point(s) on the curve $y=3\log_e x+x^2-7x$, where $x>0$.
Hence, determine the nature of each of the stationary point(s)

solutions.latex:
Differentiating:

$$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{3}{x}+2x-7$$

Stationary points occur when $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=0$:

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{3}{x}+2x-7&=0\\ 2x^2-7x+3&=0 &&(\text{multiply by } x)\\ (2x-1)(x-3)&=0 \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ x=\dfrac{1}{2} \text{ or } x=3$$

solutions.latex:
Differentiating again:

$$\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=-\dfrac{3}{x^2}+2$$

At $x=\dfrac{1}{2}$:

$$\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=-3\times4+2=-10<0$$

so there is a maximum turning point at $x=\dfrac{1}{2}$.

At $x=3$:

$$\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=-\dfrac{3}{9}+2=\dfrac{5}{3}>0$$

so there is a minimum turning point at $x=3$.

Differentiating:

$$y'=12x^3-12x^2=12x^2(x-1)$$

$$y''=36x^2-24x$$

For stationary points, $y'=0$, so $x=0$ or $x=1$.

When $x=0$, $y=2$. When $x=1$, $y=3-4+2=1$.

At $x=0$: $y''(0)=0$, so the second derivative test is inconclusive. Since $12x^2\ge 0$ and $x-1<0$ near $x=0$, $y'$ is negative on both sides of $x=0$, so the curve does not change direction.

Hence $(0,2)$ is a horizontal point of inflection.

$$\therefore\ \text{minimum at }(1,1),\ \text{horizontal point of inflection at }(0,2)$$

$$\begin{aligned} u&=2-x & v&=(x+2)^3\\ u'&=-1 & v'&=3(x+2)^2\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x) &= -(x+2)^3+(2-x)\times3(x+2)^2 \\ &= (x+2)^2\left[3(2-x)-(x+2)\right] \\ &= (x+2)^2(6-3x-x-2) \\ &= (x+2)^2(4-4x) \\ &= 4(x+2)^2(1-x) \end{aligned}$$
as required.

A maximum turning point at $(2,8)$ means $f'(2)=0$.

$$\begin{aligned} 8 &= 2\times 2^2(k-2) \\ 8 &= 8(k-2) \\ 1 &= k-2 \\ k &= 3 \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Show that the curve $y=x^2-8\ln x$ is concave up for all values of $x>0$.

solutions.latex:
Differentiate twice.
$$\begin{aligned} y&=x^2-8\ln x\\ \dfrac{dy}{dx}&=2x-\dfrac{8}{x}\\ \dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}&=2+\dfrac{8}{x^2} \end{aligned}$$
For $x>0$, $\dfrac{8}{x^2}>0$, so $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}>2>0$.

Therefore the curve is concave up for all $x>0$.
criteria: Substantial progress, e.g. finds the first derivative, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Find the coordinates and nature of the stationary points on the curve $y=\dfrac{x^2}{x-2}$.

solutions.latex:
Use the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x^2 & v&=x-2\\ u'&=2x & v'&=1\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dy}{dx} &= \dfrac{2x(x-2)-x^2}{(x-2)^2} \\ &= \dfrac{x^2-4x}{(x-2)^2} \\ &= \dfrac{x(x-4)}{(x-2)^2} \end{aligned}$$
Stationary points occur where $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=0$, so $x=0$ or $x=4$.

When $x=0$, $y=0$. When $x=4$, $y=8$.

Stationary points are $(0,0)$ and $(4,8)$.

The sign of $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ decides the nature (the curve is undefined at $x=2$):
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dy}{dx} &> 0 &&\text{for } x<0 &&\text{increasing}\\ \dfrac{dy}{dx} &= 0 &&\text{at } x=0 \\ \dfrac{dy}{dx} &< 0 &&\text{for } 0<x<2 \text{ and } 2<x<4 &&\text{decreasing}\\ \dfrac{dy}{dx} &= 0 &&\text{at } x=4 \\ \dfrac{dy}{dx} &> 0 &&\text{for } x>4 &&\text{increasing}\end{aligned}$$
Therefore $(0,0)$ is a maximum turning point and $(4,8)$ is a minimum turning point.
criteria: Finds the stationary points and the nature of one of them, or equivalent merit
Finds the stationary points, or equivalent merit
Applies the quotient rule for differentiation, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Use calculus to determine and verify the nature of the stationary points, find local maxima and minima and points of inflection (horizontal or otherwise) and hence sketch the graph of the function $y=12x^5-15x^4-40x^3$. Accurate values for all $x$-intercepts are not required.

solutions.latex:
Differentiate and factorise.
$$\begin{aligned}y&=12x^5-15x^4-40x^3\\y'&=60x^4-60x^3-120x^2\\&=60x^2(x-2)(x+1)\end{aligned}$$
Stationary points occur when $y'=0$, so $x=0,\ 2,\ -1$.
$$\begin{aligned}y''&=240x^3-180x^2-240x\\&=60x(4x^2-3x-4)\end{aligned}$$
Test each stationary point using $y''$.
$$\begin{aligned}x=0&: y''=0 &&\text{(possible inflection)}\\x=2&: y''=720>0 &&\text{(concave up, minimum)}\\x=-1&: y''=-180<0 &&\text{(concave down, maximum)}\end{aligned}$$
Possible inflections occur when $y''=0$: $x=0$ or $4x^2-3x-4=0$, giving
$$x=\dfrac{3\pm\sqrt{73}}{8}\approx-0.69 \text{ or } 1.44$$
Test the concavity either side.
$$\begin{aligned}x=-0.5&: y''=45>0\\x=1&: y''=-180<0\end{aligned}$$
Concavity changes at each of these, so all are points of inflection. At $x=0$ the gradient is also zero, so it is a horizontal inflection.

Key points: local maximum $(-1,13)$, point of inflection $(-0.693,7.935)$, horizontal inflection $(0,0)$, point of inflection $(1.443,-110.143)$, local minimum $(2,-176)$.

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=(x+3) & v&=(x-1)^2\\ u'&=1 & v'&=2(x-1)\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x) &= (x+3)\cdot 2(x-1)+(x-1)^2\times 1 \\ &= 3x^2+2x-5 \end{aligned}$$

$$x=-\dfrac{5}{3}\text{ or }x=1$$
When $x=-\dfrac{5}{3}$, $y=\dfrac{256}{27}$. When $x=1$, $y=0$.

$$\begin{aligned} \text{At } x=-\dfrac{5}{3}:\ f''&=6\times\left(-\dfrac{5}{3}\right)+2=-8<0 &&\text{maximum}\\ \text{At } x=1:\ f''&=6\times 1+2=8>0 &&\text{minimum}\end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: The graph of $y=\dfrac{1}{3}x^3-4x^2-9x+5$ has a local maximum turning point at:

solutions.latex:
Differentiate and find the stationary points.

$$\begin{aligned} y' &= x^2-8x-9\\ &= (x-9)(x+1) \end{aligned}$$

So $y'=0$ at $x=-1$ and $x=9$.

The second derivative decides the nature.

$$y''=2x-8$$

At $x=-1$, $y''=-10<0$, so there is a local maximum.

The $y$-value there is

$$\begin{aligned} y &= -\dfrac{1}{3}-4+9+5\\ &= 9\dfrac{2}{3} \end{aligned}$$

The local maximum is at $\left(-1,\ 9\dfrac{2}{3}\right)$, which is option A.

parts.latex: Find the first and second derivative of the function $f(x)=(x^2-4)^3$.

solutions.latex:
Use the chain rule for the first derivative.

$$\begin{aligned} f'(x) &= 3(x^2-4)^2\times 2x\\ &= 6x(x^2-4)^2 \end{aligned}$$

Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with

$$\begin{aligned} u&=6x & v&=(x^2-4)^2\\ u'&=6 & v'&=4x(x^2-4)\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} f''(x) &= 6(x^2-4)^2+6x\times 4x(x^2-4)\\ &= 6(x^2-4)\left[(x^2-4)+4x^2\right]\\ &= 6(x^2-4)(5x^2-4) \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ f'(x)=6x(x^2-4)^2 \text{ and } f''(x)=6(x^2-4)(5x^2-4)$$
criteria: Finds $f'(x)$ and applies the product rule for $f''(x)$, or equivalent merit

Stationary points occur where $f'(x)=0$.

$$\begin{aligned} f'(x) &= 4x^3-6x\\ &= 2x(2x^2-3) \end{aligned}$$

So $x=0$ or $x=\pm\sqrt{\dfrac{3}{2}}$.

$$f(0)=0$$

$$\begin{aligned} f\left(\pm\sqrt{\dfrac{3}{2}}\right) &= \dfrac{9}{4}-\dfrac{9}{2}\\ &= -2\dfrac{1}{4} \end{aligned}$$

solutions.latex:
As $x\to\pm\infty$, the denominator grows without bound, so $f(x)\to 0$.

solutions.latex:

Show that there are NO stationary points.
Determine the behaviour of the curve as $x\to\infty$ and as $x\to-\infty.$
Hence sketch the curve $y=\dfrac{e^x}{e^x+1}$

solutions.latex:
For the $y$-intercept, put $x=0$:
$$y=\dfrac{e^0}{e^0+1}=\dfrac{1}{2}$$
For the $x$-intercept, put $y=0$:
$$\dfrac{e^x}{e^x+1}=0$$
But $e^x\ne 0$ for all $x$, so there is no solution.

$$\therefore\ y\text{-intercept }\dfrac{1}{2},\ \text{no }x\text{-intercept}$$
criteria: Finds the $y$-intercept or shows no $x$-intercept, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=e^x & v&=e^x+1\\ u'&=e^x & v'&=e^x\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} y'&=\dfrac{(e^x+1)e^x-e^x\cdot e^x}{(e^x+1)^2}\\ &=\dfrac{e^x(e^x+1-e^x)}{(e^x+1)^2}\\ &=\dfrac{e^x}{(e^x+1)^2}\end{aligned}$$
For stationary points $y'=0$:
$$\dfrac{e^x}{(e^x+1)^2}=0$$
But $e^x\ne 0$ for all $x$, so there is no solution.

$$\therefore\ \text{there are no stationary points}$$

As $x\to\infty$, $e^x$ becomes very large, so $y\to 1$ from below.

As $x\to-\infty$, $e^x\to 0$, so $y\to 0$ from above.
$$\therefore\ y\to 1^{-}\text{ as }x\to\infty,\quad y\to 0^{+}\text{ as }x\to-\infty$$
criteria: Correct behaviour in one direction, or equivalent merit

Stationary points occur where $f'(x)=0$.

Find the coordinates of any horizontal points of inflexion on the curve with equation

solutions.latex:
Differentiate twice.
$$\begin{aligned}y&=x^4-8x^3+18x^2+4\\\dfrac{dy}{dx}&=4x^3-24x^2+36x\\\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}&=12x^2-48x+36\end{aligned}$$
Possible points of inflexion occur where $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=0$.
$$\begin{aligned}0&=12x^2-48x+36\\0&=x^2-4x+3\\0&=(x-3)(x-1)\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x=1\text{ or }x=3$$
For a horizontal point of inflexion, the value of $x$ must also be a stationary point, so $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=0$.

When $x=1$:
$$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=4(1)^3-24(1)^2+36(1)=16\ne 0$$
When $x=3$:
$$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=4(3)^3-24(3)^2+36(3)=0$$
So only $x=3$ is stationary. Check for a change of concavity:

\extable{Ts6037_1}

When $x=3$:
$$\begin{aligned}y&=3^4-8(3)^3+18(3)^2+4\\&=31\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ (3,31)\text{ is a horizontal point of inflexion}$$

Differentiate $f(x)=x^2-7x+5\ln x+8$.
$$f'(x)=2x-7+\dfrac{5}{x}$$
Stationary points occur where $f'(x)=0$.
$$\begin{aligned}0&=2x-7+\dfrac{5}{x}\\0&=2x^2-7x+5\\0&=2x^2-2x-5x+5\\0&=2x(x-1)-5(x-1)\\0&=(2x-5)(x-1)\end{aligned}$$
$$x=1\text{ or }x=\dfrac{5}{2}$$
When $x=1$:
$$\begin{aligned}f(1)&=1-7+5\ln 1+8\\&=2\end{aligned}$$
When $x=\dfrac{5}{2}$:
$$\begin{aligned}f\left(\dfrac{5}{2}\right)&=\left(\dfrac{5}{2}\right)^2-7\left(\dfrac{5}{2}\right)+5\ln\left(\dfrac{5}{2}\right)+8\\&=5\ln\left(\dfrac{5}{2}\right)-\dfrac{13}{4}\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ A(1,2),\quad B\left(\dfrac{5}{2},\ 5\ln\left(\dfrac{5}{2}\right)-\dfrac{13}{4}\right)$$

The factor $-2$ reflects the graph in the $x$-axis, so the local maximum at $A$ becomes a local minimum.
$$\therefore\ A_1=(2,-4),\text{ a local minimum}$$

Find coordinates of any points of inflection.

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=2x & v&=e^{\frac{x}{2}}\\ u'&=2 & v'&=\dfrac{1}{2}e^{\frac{x}{2}}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x) &= 2e^{\frac{x}{2}}+xe^{\frac{x}{2}} \\ &= (2+x)e^{\frac{x}{2}} \end{aligned}$$
Stationary points occur when $f'(x)=0$. Since $e^{\frac{x}{2}}>0$, this needs $2+x=0$, so $x=-2$.
$$f(-2)=-\dfrac{4}{e}\approx -1.47$$
Test the sign of $f'(x)$ either side of $x=-2$:

\extable{Ts6126_1}

The gradient changes from negative to positive.
$$\therefore\ \text{there is a minimum turning point at } \left(-2,-\dfrac{4}{e}\right)$$

solutions.latex:
From part (a), $f'(x)=(2+x)e^{\frac{x}{2}}$.

Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=2+x & v&=e^{\frac{x}{2}}\\ u'&=1 & v'&=\dfrac{1}{2}e^{\frac{x}{2}}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} f''(x) &= e^{\frac{x}{2}}+\dfrac{2+x}{2}e^{\frac{x}{2}} \\ &= e^{\frac{x}{2}}\left(1+\dfrac{2+x}{2}\right) \\ &= e^{\frac{x}{2}}\left(\dfrac{4+x}{2}\right) \end{aligned}$$
Since $e^{\frac{x}{2}}>0$, $f''(x)=0$ when $4+x=0$, so $x=-4$.

Test the sign of $f''(x)$ either side of $x=-4$:

\extable{Ts6127_1}

The concavity changes at $x=-4$.
$$f(-4)=-\dfrac{8}{e^2}\approx -1.083$$
$$\therefore\ \text{there is a point of inflection at } \left(-4,-\dfrac{8}{e^2}\right)$$

From part (b), $f''(x)=e^{\frac{x}{2}}\left(\dfrac{4+x}{2}\right)$ and $e^{\frac{x}{2}}>0$.

The curve is concave down when $f''(x)<0$, that is when $4+x<0$.
$$\therefore\ x<-4$$

parts.latex: Given $f(x)=\dfrac{1}{x}$ and $g(x)=x^2-4$, find the equation of any vertical asymptotes of $f(g(x))$.

solutions.latex:
Substituting $g(x)$ into $f$:

$$f(g(x))=\dfrac{1}{x^2-4}$$

Vertical asymptotes occur where the denominator is zero.

$$\begin{aligned} x^2-4&=0\\ (x-2)(x+2)&=0\end{aligned}$$

The numerator is never zero, so these are asymptotes.

$$\therefore\ x=2 \text{ and } x=-2$$

parts.latex: Find the stationary points on the curve $y=f(x)$ and determine their nature.
Sketch the graph, showing clearly the stationary points and any axis intercepts.

solutions.latex:
Differentiating $f(x)=4x^3-x^4$:

$$\begin{aligned} f'(x)&=12x^2-4x^3\\ &=4x^2(3-x)\end{aligned}$$

Stationary points occur where $f'(x)=0$, so $x=0$ or $x=3$.

$$f(0)=0,\qquad f(3)=4(27)-81=27$$

The stationary points are $(0,0)$ and $(3,27)$.

Nature: the second derivative is

$$f''(x)=24x-12x^2=12x(2-x)$$

At $x=3$: $f''(3)=12(3)(-1)=-36<0$, so $(3,27)$ is a local maximum.

At $x=0$: $f''(0)=0$, so the test is inconclusive and we test the sign of $f'(x)=4x^2(3-x)$ either side.

$$\begin{aligned} f'(-1)&=4(1)(4)=16>0\\ f'(1)&=4(1)(2)=8>0\end{aligned}$$

The gradient is positive on both sides of $x=0$, so $(0,0)$ is a horizontal point of inflection.

$$\therefore\ (3,27)\text{ is a local maximum and }(0,0)\text{ is a horizontal point of inflection}$$

parts.latex: Find the $x$ value of the maximum turning point on the curve $f(x)=\cos x-\sin x$ between $[0,2\pi]$.

solutions.latex:
Turning points occur where $f'(x)=0$.
$$f'(x) = -\sin x - \cos x$$
$$\begin{aligned} -\sin x - \cos x &= 0 \\ \tan x &= -1 \end{aligned}$$
For $0 \le x \le 2\pi$, $\tan x = -1$ gives $x = \dfrac{3\pi}{4}$ or $x = \dfrac{7\pi}{4}$.

The second derivative decides the nature of each point.
$$f''(x) = -\cos x + \sin x$$
$$\begin{aligned} f''\left(\dfrac{3\pi}{4}\right) &= \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2} + \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2} = \sqrt{2} > 0 &&\text{minimum}\\ f''\left(\dfrac{7\pi}{4}\right) &= -\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2} - \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2} = -\sqrt{2} < 0 &&\text{maximum} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x = \dfrac{7\pi}{4}$$
criteria: Solves $f'(x)=0$ for both values of $x$, or equivalent merit
Finds $f'(x)=-\sin x-\cos x$, or equivalent merit

4280.stem: The function $f(x) = \dfrac{x^3}{6} - \dfrac{x^2}{4} - 3x + 1$ is defined for $x$ in the domain $[-4, 6]$.

parts.latex: Find the stationary points and determine their nature.
Find the absolute maximum of $f(x)$.
Sketch $f(x)$ showing the stationary points and both endpoints.

solutions.latex:
Differentiate to find the stationary points.
$$f'(x)=\dfrac{x^2}{2}-\dfrac{x}{2}-3$$
Stationary points occur when $f'(x)=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 0 &= \dfrac{x^2}{2}-\dfrac{x}{2}-3 \\ 0 &= x^2-x-6 \\ &= (x-3)(x+2) \end{aligned}$$
So $x=-2$ or $x=3$.

The $y$ values:
$$\begin{aligned} f(-2) &= \dfrac{(-2)^3}{6}-\dfrac{(-2)^2}{4}-3(-2)+1 \\ &= -\dfrac{4}{3}-1+6+1 \\ &= 4\dfrac{2}{3} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} f(3) &= \dfrac{3^3}{6}-\dfrac{3^2}{4}-3(3)+1 \\ &= \dfrac{27}{6}-\dfrac{9}{4}-9+1 \\ &= -5\dfrac{3}{4} \end{aligned}$$
Use the second derivative to determine the nature.
$$f''(x)=x-\dfrac{1}{2}$$
$$\begin{aligned} f''(-2) &= -2-\dfrac{1}{2}=-2\dfrac{1}{2}<0 \\ f''(3) &= 3-\dfrac{1}{2}=2\dfrac{1}{2}>0 \end{aligned}$$
So there is a local maximum at $\left(-2,\,4\dfrac{2}{3}\right)$ and a local minimum at $\left(3,\,-5\dfrac{3}{4}\right)$.
criteria: Correct answer (values of $f''(-2)$ and $f''(3)$ must be given to determine nature; if a table of values is used, numerical values of $f'(x)$ must be given)
Correct derivative and finds both stationary points, including the $y$ values, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The absolute maximum on $[-4,6]$ is the greatest of the local maximum and the endpoint values. The local maximum is $4\dfrac{2}{3}$, so evaluate the endpoints.
$$\begin{aligned} f(-4) &= \dfrac{(-4)^3}{6}-\dfrac{(-4)^2}{4}-3(-4)+1 \\ &= -10\dfrac{2}{3}-4+12+1 \\ &= -1\dfrac{2}{3} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} f(6) &= \dfrac{6^3}{6}-\dfrac{6^2}{4}-3(6)+1 \\ &= 36-9-18+1 \\ &= 10 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the absolute maximum of } f(x) \text{ is } 10$$

parts.latex: A pupil is asked to find the $x$-values of any possible points of inflection for the function $f(x)=2x^3+12x^2+6x-2$. What should his answer be?

solutions.latex:
For a point of inflection, $f''(x)=0$ and the concavity changes.

Differentiating:
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x)&=6x^2+24x+6 \\ f''(x)&=12x+24 \end{aligned}$$
Setting $f''(x)=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 12x+24&=0 \\ x&=-2 \end{aligned}$$
Since $f''(x)$ is linear, it changes sign at $x=-2$.

Hence the answer is option B, $x=-2$.

parts.latex: Find any stationary points and determine their nature.
Sketch the curve, showing all main features, including intercepts, stationary points and any points of inflection.

solutions.latex:
Differentiating:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dy}{dx}&=3x^2+12x+9 \\ &=3(x^2+4x+3) \\ &=3(x+3)(x+1) \end{aligned}$$
$$\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=6x+12$$
Stationary points occur when $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=0$:
$$3(x+3)(x+1)=0$$
So $x=-3$ or $x=-1$.

For $x=-3$:
$$\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=6(-3)+12=-6<0$$
So there is a maximum at $(-3,0)$.

For $x=-1$:
$$\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=6(-1)+12=6>0$$
So there is a minimum at $(-1,-4)$.
criteria: Finds the maximum and minimum points, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Values $y(-3)=0$ and $y(-1)=-4$ checked.

solutions.latex:
Points of inflection occur where $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=0$ and the concavity changes.
$$\begin{aligned} 6x+12&=0 \\ x&=-2 \end{aligned}$$
Substituting:
$$\begin{aligned} y&=(-2)^3+6(-2)^2+9(-2) \\ &=-8+24-18 \\ &=-2 \end{aligned}$$
Testing the concavity:
$$\begin{aligned} x=-3:&\ \dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=-6<0 &&\text{concave down}\\ x=-2:&\ \dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=0 &&\\ x=-1:&\ \dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=6>0 &&\text{concave up} \end{aligned}$$
The concavity changes, so there is a point of inflection at $(-2,-2)$.

solutions.latex:
The graph of $f'(x)$ is read from the gradient of $y=f(x)$.

Stationary points of $f$ (horizontal tangents) are where $f'(x)=0$: a minimum at $x=-3$, a maximum at $x=0$ and a minimum at $x=2$.

The sign of $f'$ comes from whether $f$ is increasing or decreasing:
$$\begin{aligned}f'(x)&<0 &&\text{for } x<-3 &&f \text{ decreasing}\\ f'(x)&>0 &&\text{for } -3<x<0 &&f \text{ increasing}\\ f'(x)&<0 &&\text{for } 0<x<2 &&f \text{ decreasing}\\ f'(x)&>0 &&\text{for } x>2 &&f \text{ increasing}\end{aligned}$$

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=10x & v&=e^{-x}\\ u'&=10 & v'&=-e^{-x}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x) &= 10e^{-x}-10xe^{-x} \\ &= 10e^{-x}(1-x) \end{aligned}$$
Stationary points occur when $f'(x)=0$. Since $e^{-x}>0$, this requires $1-x=0$, so $x=1$.
$$f(1)=10e^{-1}=\dfrac{10}{e}$$
To find the nature, differentiate again, using the product rule on $10e^{-x}(1-x)$:
$$\begin{aligned} f''(x) &= -10e^{-x}(1-x)+10e^{-x}(-1) \\ &= 10e^{-x}(x-2) \end{aligned}$$
$$f''(1)=10e^{-1}(-1)=-\dfrac{10}{e}<0$$
So the curve is concave down at $x=1$.
$$\therefore\ \left(1,\dfrac{10}{e}\right)\text{ is a maximum turning point.}$$

Differentiate:

Stationary points occur when $y'=0$, so $x=0$ or $x=3$.

When $x=0$, $y=0$. When $x=3$, $y=-\dfrac{27}{4}$.

so this is a minimum point.

parts.latex: Which of the following statements is true for the function $f(x)=e^{\frac{2}{x}}-1$?

solutions.latex:
Differentiate:
$$f'(x)=-\dfrac{2}{x^2}e^{\frac{2}{x}}$$
A: $f'(1)=-2e^2$ exists, so $f$ is differentiable at $x=1$. A is false.

B: $f(0)$ is undefined because of $e^{\frac{2}{0}}$, so $f$ is not continuous at $x=0$. B is true.

C: $f'(x)=0$ has no solution, so there is no stationary point. C is false.

D: as $x\to\infty$ and as $x\to-\infty$, $f(x)\to 0$, so the horizontal asymptote is $y=0$, not $y=-1$. D is false.

Hence the answer is option B.

parts.latex: What is the nature and coordinates of the stationary point of the curve $y = \dfrac{\ln x}{x^3}$?

solutions.latex:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=\ln x & v&=x^3\\ u'&=\dfrac{1}{x} & v'&=3x^2\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} y' &= \dfrac{u'v - uv'}{v^2} \\ &= \dfrac{x^2 - 3x^2\ln x}{x^6} \\ &= \dfrac{1 - 3\ln x}{x^4} \end{aligned}$$
Stationary points occur when $y'=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 1 - 3\ln x &= 0 \\ \ln x &= \dfrac{1}{3} \\ x &= e^{\frac{1}{3}} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} y &= \dfrac{\ln e^{\frac{1}{3}}}{\left(e^{\frac{1}{3}}\right)^3} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{3e} \end{aligned}$$
The stationary point is a maximum turning point at $\left(e^{\frac{1}{3}}, \dfrac{1}{3e}\right)$, option D.

solutions.latex:
Differentiate:
$$\begin{aligned} y' &= 8x - 6x^2 = 2x(4 - 3x) \\ y'' &= 8 - 12x \end{aligned}$$
Stationary points: $y' = 0$, so $x = 0$ or $x = \dfrac{4}{3}$.

solutions.latex:
The graph is concave up when $f''(x)>0$.
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x)&=6x^2-6x \\ f''(x)&=12x-6 \end{aligned}$$
So $12x-6>0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 12x&>6 \\ x&>\dfrac{1}{2} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{concave up when } x>\dfrac{1}{2}$$
criteria: Finds $f''(x)$ and uses $f''(x)>0$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned} f(x)&=0 \\ 2x^3-3x^2&=0 \\ x^2(2x-3)&=0 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x=0 \text{ or } x=\dfrac{3}{2}$$

Stationary points occur when $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 6x^2-6x&=0 \\ 6x(x-1)&=0 \end{aligned}$$
So $x=0$ or $x=1$.

When $x=0$, $y=0$. When $x=1$, $y=2(1)^3-3(1)^2=-1$.

Hence the stationary points are $(0,0)$ and $(1,-1)$.

To find their nature, use $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=12x-6$.

When $x=0$, $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=-6<0$ (concave down), so $(0,0)$ is a maximum turning point.

When $x=1$, $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=6>0$ (concave up), so $(1,-1)$ is a minimum turning point.
criteria: Finds both stationary points, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
A point of inflexion occurs where $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=0$ and the concavity changes.
$$\begin{aligned} 12x-6&=0 \\ x&=\dfrac{1}{2} \end{aligned}$$
When $x=\dfrac{1}{2}$:
$$\begin{aligned} y&=2\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^3-3\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^2 \\ &=\dfrac{1}{4}-\dfrac{3}{4} \\ &=-\dfrac{1}{2} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{point of inflexion is } \left(\dfrac{1}{2},-\dfrac{1}{2}\right)$$

NB: The concavity changes either side of $\left(\dfrac{1}{2},-\dfrac{1}{2}\right)$. There is no need to check this, since the question states there is a point of inflexion.

solutions.latex:
Use the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x^2 & v&=e^{-x}\\ u'&=2x & v'&=-e^{-x}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x) &= 2xe^{-x}-x^2e^{-x} \\ &= xe^{-x}(2-x) \end{aligned}$$

At a stationary point $f'(x)=0$.
$$xe^{-x}(2-x)=0$$
Since $e^{-x}\ne0$, $x=0$ or $x=2$. B is the maximum, not the point at $x=0$, so $x=2$.
$$\begin{aligned} f(2) &= 2^2e^{-2} \\ &= 4e^{-2} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ y=4e^{-2}$$

solutions.latex:
Points of inflexion occur where $f''(x)=0$.
$$f''(x)=(x^2-4x+2)e^{-x}=0$$
Since $e^{-x}\ne0$, $x^2-4x+2=0$. Using the quadratic formula:
$$\begin{aligned} x &= \dfrac{4\pm\sqrt{16-4(1)(2)}}{2} \\ &= \dfrac{4\pm\sqrt8}{2} \\ &= 2\pm\sqrt2 \end{aligned}$$
C is the point with the greater $x$ value.
$$\therefore\ x=2+\sqrt2$$

parts.latex:
A curve is defined by $f(x) = \dfrac{1}{4}x^4 - 2x^2 + 1$.

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{1550_q34_s1}

Differentiating:

$$f'(x) = x^3 - 4x, \quad f''(x) = 3x^2 - 4$$

Stationary points occur when $f'(x) = 0$:

$$\begin{aligned} x^3 - 4x &= 0 \\ x(x + 2)(x - 2) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$

So $x = 0, 2, -2$, with $f(0) = 1$ and $f(\pm 2) = -3$.

Nature, using $f''$:

$$\begin{aligned} f''(0) &= -4 < 0 &&\text{so } (0, 1) \text{ is a maximum} \\ f''(-2) &= 8 > 0 &&\text{so } (-2, -3) \text{ is a minimum} \\ f''(2) &= 8 > 0 &&\text{so } (2, -3) \text{ is a minimum} \end{aligned}$$

Possible inflections occur when $f''(x) = 0$:

$$\begin{aligned} 3x^2 - 4 &= 0 \\ x^2 &= \dfrac{4}{3} \\ x &= \pm\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}} \end{aligned}$$

At both, $f(x) = -\dfrac{11}{9}$.

Test the concavity change:

$$\begin{aligned} f''(x) &> 0 &&\text{for } -2 < x < -\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}} &&\text{concave up} \\ f''(x) &< 0 &&\text{for } -\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}} < x < \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}} &&\text{concave down} \\ f''(x) &> 0 &&\text{for } \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}} < x < 2 &&\text{concave up} \end{aligned}$$

The concavity changes at each, so $\left(\pm\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}}, -\dfrac{11}{9}\right)$ are points of inflection.

$$\therefore\ f(x) \text{ is concave down for } -\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}} < x < \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}}$$

The gradient goes $-,0,+$, so $(0,0)$ is a minimum turning point.

Alternatively,
$$f''(x)=\dfrac{2-2x^2}{(x^2+1)^2}$$
and $f''(0)=2>0$, so $(0,0)$ is a minimum turning point.

parts.latex: If $y=\tan^2x$, find the values of the constants $a$ and $b$, such that $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=ay^2+by+2$.

solutions.latex:
Differentiate using the chain rule, then write in terms of $\tan x$ using $\sec^2x=1+\tan^2x$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dy}{dx}&=2\tan x\sec^2x \\ &=2\tan x(1+\tan^2x) \\ &=2\tan x+2\tan^3x \end{aligned}$$
Differentiate again.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}&=2\sec^2x+6\tan^2x\sec^2x \\ &=2(1+\tan^2x)+6\tan^2x(1+\tan^2x) \\ &=2+2\tan^2x+6\tan^2x+6\tan^4x \\ &=2+8\tan^2x+6\tan^4x \end{aligned}$$
Substitute $y=\tan^2x$.
$$\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=6y^2+8y+2$$
$$\therefore\ a=6,\ b=8$$
criteria: Finds $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}$ in terms of $\tan x$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Find the coordinates of any stationary points and determine their nature.
Determine the coordinates of its point(s) of inflexion.
Draw a sketch of the curve $y=f(x)$ in the domain $-4\le x\le 1$ clearly showing all essential features.
What is the global maximum value of the curve in the domain $-4\le x\le 1$

solutions.latex:
$$f'(x)=3x^2+12x+9,\qquad f''(x)=6x+12$$
Stationary points occur where $f'(x)=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}3(x^2+4x+3)&=0\\(x+3)(x+1)&=0\end{aligned}$$
So $x=-3$ or $x=-1$.

For $x=-3$: $y=4$ and $f''(-3)=-6<0$, so there is a maximum turning point at $(-3,4)$.

For $x=-1$: $y=0$ and $f''(-1)=6>0$, so there is a minimum turning point at $(-1,0)$.
criteria: Finds both points, or equivalent merit
Finds $f'(x)$ and sets it to zero, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
A possible point of inflexion is where $f''(x)=0$:
$$6x+12=0$$
So $x=-2$ and $y=2$.

Test the concavity:
$$\begin{aligned}f''(-3)&=-6<0 &&\text{concave down}\\f''(-2)&=0\\f''(-1)&=6>0 &&\text{concave up}\end{aligned}$$
The concavity changes, so there is a point of inflexion at $(-2,2)$.

The endpoints are $(-4,0)$ and $(1,20)$, the $y$-intercept is $4$, and the turning points and inflexion are from parts (a) and (b).

solutions.latex:

$$\therefore\ \text{global maximum}=20$$
