5344.stem: Consider the curve $y = \sin x + \cos x$ in the domain $-\pi \le x \le \pi$.

figures.cap: solution sketch: hand-drawn sketch of y = sin x + cos x on [-pi, pi]

parts.latex: Find $x$-intercepts, express your answer in terms of $\pi$.
Find any stationary points, and determine their nature.
Find any points of inflection.
Explain why the points found in (c) are not points of horizontal inflection.
Hence, sketch the graph of $y = \sin x + \cos x$, for $-\pi \le x \le \pi$, showing all critical features of the graph.

solutions.latex:
The $x$-intercepts occur where $y=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} \sin x + \cos x &= 0 \\ \sin x &= -\cos x \\ \tan x &= -1 \end{aligned}$$
In $-\pi \le x \le \pi$:
$$\therefore\ x = -\dfrac{\pi}{4} \text{ or } x = \dfrac{3\pi}{4}$$
criteria: One correct intercept, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Stationary points occur where $y'=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} y' &= \cos x - \sin x = 0 \\ \tan x &= 1 \end{aligned}$$
So $x = \dfrac{\pi}{4}$ or $x = -\dfrac{3\pi}{4}$.

Test the nature with the second derivative:
$$y'' = -\sin x - \cos x$$
At $x = \dfrac{\pi}{4}$:
$$y'' = -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} - \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} < 0 \quad \text{(maximum)}$$
At $x = -\dfrac{3\pi}{4}$:
$$y'' = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} + \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} > 0 \quad \text{(minimum)}$$
The $y$-values are:
$$y\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} + \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} = \sqrt{2}, \qquad y\left(-\dfrac{3\pi}{4}\right) = -\sqrt{2}$$
$$\therefore\ \left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}, \sqrt{2}\right) \text{ is a local maximum and } \left(-\dfrac{3\pi}{4}, -\sqrt{2}\right) \text{ is a local minimum.}$$
criteria: Finds the nature of both points, or equivalent merit
Finds the maximum or the minimum, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Points of inflection occur where $y''=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} -\sin x - \cos x &= 0 \\ \tan x &= -1 \end{aligned}$$
So $x = -\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ or $x = \dfrac{3\pi}{4}$.

Test concavity:

\extable{Ts8070_1}

Since the concavity changes at each value, the points $\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{4}, 0\right)$ and $\left(\dfrac{3\pi}{4}, 0\right)$ are points of inflection.
\exfigure{1279_q24_s1}
criteria: Shows key points (maximum and minimum), or equivalent merit

meta.marker_note: Key points need to be shown (maximum, minimum); end points: all points required.

solutions.latex:
A horizontal point of inflection needs $y'=0$ as well as a change of concavity.
$$\begin{aligned} y'\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)&=\cos\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)-\sin\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}+\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}=\sqrt2\ne0 \\ y'\left(\dfrac{3\pi}{4}\right)&=-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}=-\sqrt2\ne0 \end{aligned}$$
The gradient is not zero at either point, so they are not horizontal points of inflection.
criteria: Shows $y'\ne0$ at both points of inflection

Find the coordinates of the stationary points on the curve with the equation $y=f(x)$ and determine their nature.
Sketch the graphs of $y=f(x)$ and $y=-f(x)$ on the same diagram. Clearly label each graph and showing all important features.

solutions.latex:
For the $x$-intercept, put $y=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 0&=(x-2)(x^2+1)\\ x&=2\end{aligned}$$
For the $y$-intercept, put $x=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} y&=(0-2)(0^2+1)\\ &=-2\end{aligned}$$
The intercepts are $(2,0)$ and $(0,-2)$.
criteria: Finds either the $x$ or $y$ intercept, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x-2 & v&=x^2+1\\ u'&=1 & v'&=2x\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x)&=(x-2)\cdot 2x+(x^2+1)\times1\\ &=3x^2-4x+1\\ f''(x)&=6x-4\end{aligned}$$
For stationary points, $f'(x)=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 3x^2-4x+1&=0\\ (3x-1)(x-1)&=0\end{aligned}$$
so $x=\dfrac13$ or $x=1$.

When $x=\dfrac13$, $y=-\dfrac{50}{27}$. When $x=1$, $y=-2$.

The stationary points are $\left(\dfrac13,-\dfrac{50}{27}\right)$ and $(1,-2)$.

Nature, using the sign of $f''(x)$:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{At } x=\dfrac13:\ f''&=6\times\dfrac13-4=-2<0 &&\text{maximum}\\ \text{At } x=1:\ f''&=6\times1-4=2>0 &&\text{minimum}\end{aligned}$$
So $\left(\dfrac13,-\dfrac{50}{27}\right)$ is a maximum and $(1,-2)$ is a minimum.
criteria: Finds the stationary points, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: For the curve $y=2x^2-\ln\left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right)-4$, find the coordinates of the minimum stationary point. Give your answer in exact form.

solutions.latex:
A minimum occurs where $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=0$.
$$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=4x-\dfrac{0.5}{\frac{x}{2}}=4x-\dfrac1x$$
$$\begin{aligned} 0&=4x-\dfrac1x \\ 4x^2&=1 \\ x^2&=\dfrac14 \\ x&=\pm\dfrac12 \end{aligned}$$
The logarithm needs $x>0$, so $x=\dfrac12$.
$$\begin{aligned} y&=2\left(\dfrac12\right)^2-\ln\left(\dfrac{0.5}{2}\right)-4 \\ &=\ln4-3\dfrac12 \end{aligned}$$
Test the nature:
$$\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=4+\dfrac{1}{x^2}$$
At $x=\dfrac12$, $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=4+4=8>0$, so it is a minimum.
$$\therefore\ \text{the minimum point is } \left(\dfrac12,\ \ln4-\dfrac72\right)$$
criteria: Finds the minimum value without testing for a minimum, or equivalent merit
Finds the derivative, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
Show that the first and second derivatives are respectively

$$y'=12x(x-2)^2$$

$$y''=12(x-2)(3x-2)$$

Over which interval(s) is the curve decreasing?

solutions.latex:
Differentiate $y=3x^4-16x^3+24x^2-9$:

$$\begin{aligned} y'&=12x^3-48x^2+48x \\ &=12x(x^2-4x+4) \\ &=12x(x-2)^2 \end{aligned}$$

Differentiate again:

$$\begin{aligned} y''&=36x^2-96x+48 \\ &=12(3x^2-8x+4) \\ &=12(3x-2)(x-2) \\ &=12(x-2)(3x-2) \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the first derivative, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Stationary points occur when $y'=0$:

$$12x(x-2)^2=0$$

so $x=0$ or $x=2$.

When $x=0$, $y=-9$; when $x=2$, $y=7$. The stationary points are $(0,-9)$ and $(2,7)$.

At $(0,-9)$:

$$y''=12(-2)(-2)=48>0$$

The curve is concave up, so $(0,-9)$ is a minimum.

At $(2,7)$:

$$y''=12(0)(4)=0$$

This is a possible point of inflexion, so test the concavity either side:

\extable{Ts8162_1}

The concavity changes from down to up, so $(2,7)$ is a horizontal point of inflexion.

Other possible points of inflexion occur when $y''=0$:

$$12(x-2)(3x-2)=0$$

so $x=2$ or $x=\dfrac{2}{3}$.

\extable{Ts8162_2}

The concavity changes, so $\left(\dfrac{2}{3},-\dfrac{67}{27}\right)$ is a point of inflexion.

parts.latex: Find any stationary points and determine their nature.
Sketch the curve, showing all main features, including intercepts, stationary points and any points of inflection. Use the lines below for any relevant working.

solutions.latex:
Differentiate.
$$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=3x^2+12x+9$$
Stationary points: $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 3x^2+12x+9 &= 0 \\ x^2+4x+3 &= 0 \\ (x+3)(x+1) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
So $x=-3$ or $x=-1$.
$$\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=6x+12$$
When $x=-3$:
$$\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=-6<0,\qquad y=(-3)^3+6(-3)^2+9(-3)=0$$
Therefore $(-3,0)$ is a maximum turning point.

When $x=-1$:
$$\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=6>0,\qquad y=(-1)^3+6(-1)^2+9(-1)=-4$$
Therefore $(-1,-4)$ is a minimum turning point.
criteria: Finds the coordinates of the turning points, or finds the $x$-coordinates and determines nature correctly, or equivalent merit
Correct differentiation and $x$-coordinates found, or incorrect $x$-coordinates used to determine nature or coordinates, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Possible point of inflection: $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=0$.
$$6x+12=0$$
So $x=-2$.

Test the concavity.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} &= -6 &&\text{at } x=-3 &&\text{concave down}\\ \dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} &= 0 &&\text{at } x=-2 && \\ \dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} &= 6 &&\text{at } x=-1 &&\text{concave up} \end{aligned}$$
The concavity changes, so there is a point of inflection. When $x=-2$:
$$y=(-2)^3+6(-2)^2+9(-2)=-2$$
So $(-2,-2)$ is a point of inflection.

For $x$-intercepts, $y=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} x^3+6x^2+9x &= 0 \\ x(x^2+6x+9) &= 0 \\ x(x+3)^2 &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
So $x=0$ or $x=-3$.

parts.latex: Find the stationary points and determine their nature.
Find any points of inflexion.
Sketch the graph of $y = 4x^{3} - x^{4}$. showing all important features including intercepts with the axes.

solutions.latex:
Stationary points occur where $y'=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} y'&=12x^{2}-4x^{3}\\ 0&=4x^{2}(3-x)\end{aligned}$$
so $x=0$ or $x=3$.

When $x=0$, $y=0$. When $x=3$, $y=27$.

Test the nature using $y''=24x-12x^{2}$.

At $x=0$: $y''=0$, so the test fails and $(0,0)$ is a possible horizontal point of inflexion.

At $x=3$: $y''=24(3)-12(9)=-36<0$, so $(3,27)$ is a maximum turning point.

Alternatively, test the nature using $y'$.
$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c} x & -1 & 0 & 1 \\ \hline y' & 16 & 0 & 8 \end{array}$$
The gradient is positive on both sides of $x=0$, so $(0,0)$ is a possible point of inflexion.
$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c} x & 2 & 3 & 4 \\ \hline y' & 16 & 0 & -64 \end{array}$$
The gradient changes from positive to negative, so $(3,27)$ is a maximum turning point.

parts.latex: What values of $x$ is the curve $f(x) = 2x^3 + x^2$ concave down?

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned} f(x)&=2x^3+x^2 \\ f'(x)&=6x^2+2x \\ f''(x)&=12x+2 \end{aligned}$$
The curve is concave down when $f''(x)<0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 12x+2&<0 \\ x&<-\dfrac{1}{6} \end{aligned}$$
Hence the answer is $x<-\dfrac{1}{6}$.

parts.latex: If $f(x)=\dfrac{x^2+1}{4-x^2}$ then the vertical and horizontal asymptotes are respectively:

solutions.latex:
The function is undefined when the denominator is zero.
$$4-x^2=0 \text{ gives } x=\pm 2$$
So the vertical asymptotes are $x=-2$ and $x=2$.

As $x\to\infty$, $\dfrac{x^2+1}{4-x^2}\to\dfrac{1}{-1}$, so $y\to-1$ and the horizontal asymptote is $y=-1$.

Hence the answer is B.

Consider the curve $f(x)=2x^3-x^2-4x+6$. Find the stationary points of $f(x)$ and determine their nature. Then sketch the curve, clearly labelling the stationary points.

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned} f(x)&=2x^3-x^2-4x+6 \\ f'(x)&=6x^2-2x-4=2(3x^2-x-2) \end{aligned}$$

so there is a maximum turning point at $\left(-\dfrac{2}{3},\dfrac{206}{27}\right)$.
$$f''(1)=12\times1-2=10>0$$
so there is a minimum turning point at $(1,3)$.

parts.latex: Find $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}$ .
Show that $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}\ge 2$ for all values of $x$.

solutions.latex:
Since $x^2\ge 0$ for all real $x$, we have $3x^2\ge 0$.

Adding $2$ gives $3x^2+2\ge 2$.

$$\therefore\ \dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}\ge 2 \text{ for all } x$$

The gradient of the tangent at $P(2,4)$ is the value of $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ at $x=2$.
$$\begin{aligned} m &= 2^3+2(2)-7 \\ &= 5 \end{aligned}$$
The normal is perpendicular to the tangent, so its gradient is $-\dfrac{1}{5}$.
$$\begin{aligned} y-4 &= -\dfrac{1}{5}(x-2) \\ 5y-20 &= -x+2 \\ x+5y-22 &= 0 \end{aligned}$$

Stationary points occur where $y'=0$.

Since $e^{\sin x}>0$ for all $x$, there is no solution to $e^{\sin x}=0$, so $\cos x=0$.
$$x=\dfrac{\pi}{2},\ \dfrac{3\pi}{2}\qquad(0\le x\le2\pi)$$
There are exactly 2 stationary points.

At $x=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$: $y=e^{\sin\frac{\pi}{2}}=e$.

At $x=\dfrac{3\pi}{2}$: $y=e^{-1}=\dfrac{1}{e}$.
$$\therefore\ \text{the stationary points are }\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2},e\right)\text{ and }\left(\dfrac{3\pi}{2},\dfrac{1}{e}\right)$$
criteria: Shows only 2 solutions with $e^{\sin x}\ne0$ stated, or finds the coordinates, or equivalent merit

The sign of $y'$ changes from positive to negative, so $\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2},e\right)$ is a local maximum.

Near $x=\dfrac{3\pi}{2}$:
$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c}x&\pi&\dfrac{3\pi}{2}&2\pi\\\hline y'&-1&0&1\end{array}$$
The sign of $y'$ changes from negative to positive, so $\left(\dfrac{3\pi}{2},\dfrac{1}{e}\right)$ is a local minimum.

solutions.latex:
Differentiating using the chain rule:
$$f'(x)=\dfrac{1}{x^2+1}\times2x=\dfrac{2x}{x^2+1}$$
Stationary points occur where $f'(x)=0$.
$$\dfrac{2x}{x^2+1}=0$$
so $2x=0$, giving $x=0$.

Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=2x & v&=x^2+1\\ u'&=2 & v'&=2x\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} f''(x)&=\dfrac{2(x^2+1)-2x(2x)}{(x^2+1)^2} \\ &=\dfrac{2x^2+2-4x^2}{(x^2+1)^2} \\ &=\dfrac{2(1-x^2)}{(x^2+1)^2} \end{aligned}$$
$$f''(0)=\dfrac{2(1-0^2)}{(0^2+1)^2}=2>0$$
So the curve is concave up at $x=0$, a minimum point.
$$f(0)=\ln(0^2+1)=0$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the minimum point is } (0,0)$$

Inflection points occur where $f''(x)=0$ and the concavity changes.
$$\begin{aligned} 2(1-x^2)&=0 \\ x^2&=1 \\ x&=\pm1 \end{aligned}$$
$$f(\pm1)=\ln\left((\pm1)^2+1\right)=\ln2$$
Test the sign of $f''(x)=\dfrac{2(1-x^2)}{(x^2+1)^2}$ either side:

\extable{Ts8990_1}

The concavity changes at both, so
$$\therefore\ (-1,\ln2)\text{ and }(1,\ln2)\text{ are points of inflection}$$
